en: The Blessed Lord said: O mighty-armed one, hear again from Me this supreme word.
That which I, desiring your welfare, shall speak to you who are well-disposed toward me. //1//
Śrīdhara:
The manifestations (vibhūtis) were previously described in brief in the seventh chapter and elsewhere; in the tenth chapter, they are expanded upon so that the Lord may be perceived everywhere.
Thus, first, the reality of the Supreme Lord as the object of devotion has been described in the seventh chapter and those following;
and His manifestations have been shown in brief in the seventh chapter with the words, "O son of Kuntī, I am the taste in water" (Gītā 7.8),
and so forth, and in the eighth chapter with the words, "I alone am the sacrifice here" (Gītā 8.4), and so forth.
And by the words "I am the sacrifice (*kratu*), I am the offering (*yajña*)" and so forth in the ninth chapter,

the Blessed One has now spoken the words "once again" (*bhūya eva*) with the intent of elaborating upon those very manifestations (*vibhūtayaḥ*) and describing the necessity of performing devotion to Him. He addresses him as "O Mahābāho," meaning O you whose arms are great— that is, skilled in the performance of one's own duty such as battle, or in the service of the Great One.
Listen once more to my words;
of what nature are they?
They are supreme, being centered on the Supreme Self.
They shall obtain joy through the nectar of my words alone—that which I shall speak out of a desire for your welfare, a desire for what is beneficial to you. //1//
Madhusūdana:

Thus, by the seventh, eighth, and ninth chapters, the reality of the Blessed One—the referent of the word "That"—has been shown both with attributes (*sopādhika*) and without attributes (*nirupādhika*). Furthermore, His manifestations (*vibhūtayaḥ*) serve as means for the meditation upon Him with attributes and for the knowledge of Him without attributes, as stated in the seventh chapter beginning with: "I am the taste in the waters, O son of Kuntī" (Gītā 7.8).
In the ninth chapter, these were stated in brief through such passages as, "I am the sacrifice, I am the ritual" (Gītā 9.16).

Now, their detailed exposition must be told for the purpose of meditating upon the Blessed One; furthermore, because that reality is difficult to discern, it must be stated once more for the sake of knowledge. Thus, the tenth chapter begins.
Therein, first, in order to encourage Arjuna, he says, "Once again... (bhūya eva).
Furthermore, O mighty-armed one, listen again to my supreme and most excellent word.

Desiring your welfare and wishing for you to attain what is beneficial, I—who am your most trusted friend—shall speak that which, when heard from my lips by you who are filled with joy, will bring you delight as if from drinking nectar. (1)
Viśvanātha says:
Having made known the divine knowledge, that devotion which was taught in the seventh and subsequent books was taught in the tenth book along with its secrets and its manifestations.

The very sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) that was previously described in the seventh chapter and those following— which serves as the cause for the knowledge of [the Lord] as the object of worship— is now to be elaborated in detail for the sake of the bliss of those possessed of devotion. Following the maxim, "The seers speak in indirect ways, and the indirect is dear to me" (BhP 11.21.35), the author speaks somewhat cryptically, due to its difficulty of comprehension, by using the word "furthermore" (*bhūyaḥ*).
Furthermore, the meaning is that this king of sciences, this king of secrets, is being spoken.
O Mahābāho!
Just as you have manifested the strength of your arms with supreme preeminence, so too [is this taught].
The meaning is that, in the same way, this very thing should be made manifest through the intellect by means of the strength of the intellect augmented by self-restraint (*svārdhikya*).
"Listen" (*śṛṇu*) is addressed even to one who is already listening, for the purpose of ensuring correct comprehension regarding the matter about to be stated.
"Supreme" (*paramam*) means superior even to what was previously mentioned.

They used the dative case in order to cause you great amazement, according to the rule *kriyārthopapadasya ca* (Pāṇini 2.3.14), because [the gift was intended] for one who is being pleased—that is, for one possessed of love. //1//
Baladeva:

That which was described in the seventh chapter and others as one's own sovereignty being the cause of devotion is here fully nourished in this tenth chapter by means of the narration of His manifestations.
In each preceding chapter, His own devotion, along with its ancillaries, was taught as being inseparable from the description of His own sovereignty.
Now, desiring to describe in detail His own vibhūtis— which were previously mentioned only in brief— as the unique means for the arising and growth of that devotion, the Blessed One said,
"Furthermore," O Mahābāho.
Listen once more, yet again, to My supreme word.
The expression "listen to one who is already listening" is used to ensure focused attention toward the subject to be taught.
Out of a desire for your welfare, I shall speak to you that supreme, glorious word concerning My divine manifestations.
The dative case is used according to the rule beginning with *kriyārthopapada* (Pāṇini 2.3.14).
The meaning is: "in order to cause even you, though wise, to be filled with wonder.
"Desire for welfare" (*hitakāmyayā*) refers to the longing for your well-being in the form of the arising and increase of devotion to Me.
To what kind of person? He says: "to one who is being pleased," meaning that from my words, such a person finds joy as if from drinking nectar. //1//
Neither the hosts of gods nor the great seers know my origin,
for I am the source of the gods and the great seers in every respect.
Śrīdhara: He states the reason for the difficulty of understanding even that which has already been said in the verse beginning with "na me viduḥ.
Even the hosts of gods and the great seers, such as Bhṛgu and others, do not know my supreme birth—that is, my manifestation through various glories (*vibhūtis*), even though I am devoid of birth.
The reason for this is: "For I am the origin and cause of all the gods and the great seers."
"In every way" means in all manners, both as the cause of origination and as the impeller of the intellect and other faculties.
Therefore, the meaning is that no one knows me without my grace. //2//
Madhusūdana says:

"Why do you speak again what has already been stated many times before? To this he replies, "Neither gods nor great sages know my origin. *Prabhavam* means power (*prabhāva*), the preeminence of the Lord's sovereign capacity; or it refers to his manifestation (*prabhavanam*), that is, his appearance through manifold glories (*vibhūtis*). Neither the hosts of gods, such as Indra and others, nor the great sages, such as Bhṛgu and others, know this.
Even the omniscient ones do not know Me.

He states the reason for their lack of knowledge: "For I am, in every way and in all respects, the cause of all the gods and great sages, both as their progenitor and as the efficient and material cause by means of My intellect and other faculties."
The proponent says "and so" because of this reason;
therefore, the meaning is that those who are my transformations do not know my power. //2//
Viśvanātha:
And this [state] is to be known only through the excellence of my grace and not otherwise; thus he says, "Not by me...
The hosts of gods do not know my origin—that supreme, entirely extraordinary birth of mine in Devakī.
"Let those [ordinary people] not know because they are possessed by sense objects;
but let the sages know. To this he says: "Even the great sages do not [know me]," for which the reason is: "I am the origin, the cause, in every way—that is, in all possible modes."
The sense is that sons do not know the true nature of their father's birth.

Since the subsequent restatement—"Neither the gods nor the demons, O Blessed One, know Your manifestation" (Gītā 10.14)—indicates otherwise, one should not assume here that the word *prabhava* has any other meaning. //2//
Baladeva, feeling that this is difficult to understand without compassion for His devotees, says "not by me" with this intention:

the hosts of gods, beginning with Brahmā, and the great sages, beginning with Sanaka, do not know—do not perceive—My origin, which is My manifestation through sovereignty; that is to say, they do not know My turning [into the world] by virtue of possessing an infinite, divine nature, qualities, and opulences.
To the question "Why?", he says: "I am their origin.
The meaning is that I am their origin—the primary cause—in every respect and in all ways, by virtue of being their producer and by virtue of being the giver of intellect and the rest.

Since godhood, sovereignty, and so forth were given to them by me alone when I was pleased by their respective acts of worship, they do not know me, who am established from before, nor my sovereignty.
And the Śruti says thus: "Who indeed knows? Who here has declared it? Whence was it born, and whence came this creation?"
"The gods were later than its emission;
who then knows from whence it has arisen? (Rv 8.7.17, Taitt.Br. 2.8.9.76), and "The gods did not reach that which was prior," and other such passages. //2//
He who knows me as unborn and beginningless, the Great Lord of the worlds— he,
undeluded among mortals, is liberated from all sins. (10.3)

Śrīdhara: He states the fruit of such knowledge of the Self in the verse beginning with "He who [knows] Me. Because I am the cause of all, I have no beginning—that is, no prior cause; thus I am *anādi*. For that very reason, I am *aja*, devoid of birth, and the Great Lord (*maheśvara*) of the worlds. He who knows Me as such, being among men undeluded—meaning free from delusion—is liberated from all sins. (3)
Madhusūdana says "yo mām" (he who [knows] me) because, due to its great fruit, only a rare few understand the power of the Blessed One.

Because He is the cause of all, there exists no beginning—that is, no cause—for Him; thus He is "anādi" (without beginning). And because He is without beginning, He is "aja" (unborn), meaning devoid of birth.

He who knows me as the great Lord of the worlds, among mortals he is undeluded—devoid of delusion—and is completely liberated from all sins, even those committed intentionally; he is released through the radical eradication of their causes, being freed in the form of the absence of their latent impressions (saṃskāras). //3//
Viśvanātha:

Now, since even the gods and sages know that this birth of yours—the body of the Supreme Brahman, which is unconditioned by all space and time—is indeed [your own], he touches his chest with his own index finger and says, "He who me... and so forth.

"He who knows me as unborn"—what [of him]? He knows the Supreme Lord (parameṣṭhin) as indeed beginningless, true, and therefore unborn (*aja*) because of being without beginning (*anāditva*), and thus not produced (*ajanya*). To that, he says "and" (*ca*): the meaning is that he who knows me—who am unborn (*aja*), unproduced (*ajanya*), and yet born of Vasudeva—as truly beginningless (*anādim eva*).
By the word "me" (mām), the fact of being born from Vasudeva is understood, as stated by me in the words: "My birth and action are divine" (Gītā 4.9).
That I possess birth and yet, due to being the Supreme Self, am eternally unborn—both of these are my supreme truth, established solely through inconceivable power.
As it has been said: "Though I am unborn and my nature is imperishable, I manifest myself" (Gītā 4.6).
And likewise is the speech of Uddhava: "O You who are beyond desire and beyond worldly existence, these activities of Yours cause the intellect of even the wise here to suffer" (BhP 3.4.16).
Regarding this, there is also a verse from the *Śrī-Bhāgavatāmṛta*:
"If each of those [worldly things] were not real, then the intellect of the wise would be a delusion."
"It could not be so"; therefore, an inconceivable power (*acintya-śakti*) is the cause in these divine sports (*līlā*).

Thus, just as in my childhood during the sport of being Dāmodara, it was entirely beyond logical reasoning that at one and the same time there was limitation by the binding of the small bell (*kiṅkiṇī*) and non-limitation by the rope (*dāman*) from which I was bound; in the very same way, my state of being unborn (*ajatva*) and my possessing birth are likewise beyond logical reasoning.

He speaks of sovereignty that is difficult to comprehend: "Among mortals, only he who knows You, the Great Lord of all worlds, to be the charioteer of even the Lord of the World (Lokamaheśvara), is truly undeluded;
[only he is freed] from all sins that oppose devotion.

As for those who explain that birthlessness, beginninglessness, and universal lordship alone are the actual realities, while qualities such as possessing birth are established merely through imitation—[that view is refuted by this].
The meaning is that he, being utterly deluded, is not liberated from all sins. //3//
Baladeva: With the thought that such knowledge concerning Me belongs only to someone rare, He says, "He who...

Among thousands of mortals, even though they are striving, he who is some person—by chance knowing My true nature, devoted to the company of the virtuous (sat-prasaṅgī)—knows Me as the beginningless, unborn, and the Great Lord of the world;
he, being undeluded, is liberated from all sins—this is the connection [of the verse].

In this context, by the term "unborn" (*aja*), there is a distinction from the category of insentient matter (*acid-varga*) as the primary cause (*pradhāna*) and from the category of transmigrating beings (*saṃsāri-varga*),
because the former is subject to birth through its own transformation while the latter is subject to birth through the production of a body.

When further qualified by the term "beginningless" (*anādi*), there is a distinction from the category of liberated spirits (*mukta-cid-varga*), because His state of being unborn is due to His connection with the body of the primordial God.

Because the state of being a "born one" (*janmitva*) occurs previously [in time], the phrase "the Great Lord of the World" (*loka-maheśvara*) establishes His distinction from the class of eternally liberated conscious beings (*nitya-mukta-cid-varga*) as well as from *prakṛti* and *kāla*; for although these possess beginninglessness and non-bornness (*anādy-ajatva*), they lack the status of being the Great Lord of the World.

Furthermore, by the qualification "without beginning" (*anādima*), His distinction from Brahmā (*vidhi*), Rudra, and others is established, since their status as lords of the world is only beginningless (*sāditva*) insofar as it is granted by the Supreme Lord Himself.
Thus, as explained at length elsewhere,
he who knows that [the Lord] is always devoid of any connection with what is to be abandoned and is eternally established in universal sovereignty— being thus distinct from all others—
is liberated by all actions, whether they be conducive to the arising of devotion to Me or otherwise, and attains devotion to Me.
Your cognition is "with delusion" because it is not undeluded due to its similarity to other [cognitions]; You are "devoid" of that.
Furthermore, how can there be non-birth for You who were born of Devakī? For You were born without ever abandoning Your non-birth within her. //3//
Intellect, knowledge, freedom from delusion, forgiveness, truthfulness, self-control, tranquility,
pleasure, pain, birth, non-existence, fear, and even fearlessness— 4.
Non-violence, equanimity, contentment, austerity, charity, fame, and infamy—these various states of beings arise from Me alone. (5)
Śrīdhara: He clarifies [the Lord's] very status as the Great Lord of the world with three verses beginning with "buddhiḥ.
*Buddhi* is the skill in discriminating between the essential and the non-essential;
*jñāna* is that which has the Self as its object.
Non-delusion is the absence of confusion;
forbearance is the capacity for endurance;
truth is speech that accords with reality.
Dama is the restraint of the external senses; śama is the restraint of the internal organ;
and sukha is that which is experienced as agreeable to the mind.
Suffering is the opposite of that;
existence is arising;
non-existence is the opposite of that.
Fear is terror;
fearlessness is its opposite.
The connection with the following verse is that this [fear and fearlessness] arises from me alone. //4//
Furthermore, what is non-violence? Non-violence is the cessation of harming others.
Equanimity is the absence of passion, hatred, and so forth.
Contentment is satisfaction with what is obtained by fate;
austerity is that which will be described as scriptural and so forth;
and charity is the bestowing of wealth and other goods acquired through righteous means upon a worthy recipient.
Fame is good reputation;
infamy is ill-repute.
These—such as intelligence and knowledge, as well as their opposites such as lack of intelligence and so forth—are various states that arise for living beings from Me alone, from My very self. (5)
Madhusūdana:
In two verses beginning with "Buddhi," he elaborates upon his own status as the Great Lord of the world.
"Buddhi" refers to the capacity of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) for the discernment of subtle objects.
Knowledge is the comprehension of all things, both self and non-self.
Non-delusion is the engagement with discernment, free from confusion, regarding present objects of cognition and duties to be performed.
Forbearance is the state of an unchanging mind when reviled or struck.
Truth is the speaking exactly as it is of an object known through a valid means of cognition.
Self-restraint is the withdrawal of the external senses from their respective objects. Peace is the tranquility of the internal organ.
Pleasure has dharma as its unique cause and is experienced as agreeable;
suffering has adharma as its unique cause and is experienced as disagreeable;
existence is birth.
Existence (*bhāva*) is being (*sattā*);
non-existence (*abhāva*) is non-being (*asattā*).
Fear (*bhaya*) is terror; its opposite is fearlessness (*abhaya*).
And thus, one *ca*-particle has the sense of a stated conjunction (*ukta-samuccaya*),
while the other has the sense of a conjunction of unstated factors such as the ignorance of the intellect (*abuddhi-ajñāna*) and so forth;
"thus" (*eva*) refers to these [factors] well-known to all the world.
The meaning is "thus. The connection with what follows is: "it arises from me alone. //4//
Non-violence (*ahiṃsā*) is the cessation of causing pain to living beings. Equanimity (*samatā*) is a state of mind free from attachment, aversion, and the like.
Contentment (*tuṣṭi*) is the realization that "this much is sufficient" regarding objects of enjoyment.
Austerity (*tapas*) is the emaciation of the body and the senses according to the scriptural path.
Giving (*dāna*) is the offering of wealth to a worthy recipient (*sat-pātra*) with faith, according to one's ability, at the proper place and time.
Fame (*yaśas*) is renown in the form of worldly praise based on the cause of righteousness (*dharma*).
Infamy, however, is a well-known state consisting of worldly censure caused by unrighteousness (*adharma*).
These entities, beginning with intellect (*buddhi*), are specific effects that possess causes; they are of various kinds and manifold due to the diversity of the means of *dharma* and *adharma*.
All of these arise from me alone, the Supreme Lord, for all living beings, and not from any other source.
Therefore, what need is there to speak of my status as the Great Lord of the world? This is the meaning. //5//
Viśvanātha:
Nor can those who know the scriptures determine my state of intoxication by means of their own intellect and so forth;

for since the intellect and other faculties are born from me alone—being produced from the qualities of Māyā such as *sattva* and the rest—they lack the inherent capacity to penetrate Me, who am beyond the qualities (*guṇātīta*). Thus he says: "Intellect (*buddhi*) is the capacity for determining subtle objects."
Knowledge (*jñāna*) is the discrimination between the Self and the non-Self;
lack of delusion (*asaṃmoha*) is the absence of distraction.
These three states, being considered as the causes for knowing my true nature, appear as if they were to be cultivated.
But these are not the [only] causes.
By way of illustration, he states that other entities seen in the worlds have not arisen from themselves alone: *kṣamā* is forbearance;
*satya* is speaking in accordance with reality.
Dama is the restraint of the external senses;
śama is the restraint of the internal sense.
These are the qualities of sattva.
Happiness is of the nature of goodness (sāttvika); suffering is of the nature of darkness (tāmasa).
Existence and non-existence refer to the specific miseries of birth and death.
Fear born of tamas is characterized by darkness; fearlessness arising from knowledge is characterized by sattva; that which arises from rajas and the like is characterized by rajas;
[and equanimity] is through comparison with one's own self.
Seeing pleasure, pain, and so forth everywhere with equanimity is non-violence; these two are sattvic.
Contentment is complete satisfaction;
that which is free from worldly attachment is sattvic.
But that which is with expectation is rajasic.
Even in the case of austerity and charity, there is the sattvic and the rajasic according to whether they are without expectation or with expectation;
and the same applies to fame and infamy.
"From me"—that is to say, even you, sirs, arise from me alone, because of the identity of power and the possessor of power within my own creative illusion (māyā). //4-5//
Baladeva: Now, with two verses beginning with "Buddhi," he elaborates upon his own status as the primordial source of all and as the Lord of all.
*Buddhi* is the capacity for discerning subtle objects;
*jñāna* is the discernment between conscious and unconscious entities.
Non-delusion is the absence of distraction.
Forbearance is endurance.
Truth is speech for the benefit of others concerning objects as they have been perceived.
Dama is the restraint [of the senses] from objects that cause harm, such as grief and the like;
śama is the [restraint] of the mind from those [objects];
and sukha is that which is experienced as being favorable.
Suffering, however, is to be experienced as something disagreeable;
existence is birth;
non-existence is death.
Fear (*bhaya*) is terror arising from the perception of the causes of future suffering; its cessation is fearlessness (*abhaya*). Non-violence (*ahiṃsā*) is the state of not causing pain to others.
Equanimity (*samatā*) is being devoid of attachment and aversion.
Contentment is satisfaction with what is obtained without seeking;
austerity is bodily mortification as prescribed in the Vedas;
and charity is the bestowing of one's own possessions upon a worthy recipient.
Fame is the renown of one's good qualities;
its opposite is infamy. Such states as these arise for living beings—gods, humans, and so forth—from Me alone, that is, from My will. Thus, the meaning is that I alone am their cause.
They are of various kinds and possess distinct characteristics. //4-5//
The seven great seers of old and likewise the four Manus were born from my mind, and from them these creatures in the world have descended. (10.6)
Śrīdhara: Furthermore, regarding the phrase "the great sages" (*maharṣayaḥ*):

the seven great sages, Bhṛgu and the others, are known as the "seven Brahmās"; they are established as such in the Purāṇas, as in the passage beginning with *Mbh 12.201.5*. Beyond them, there were four other great sages, Sanaka and the rest, who are well-known from the Purāṇas.
Likewise, the Manus, such as Svāyambhuva and others,
possess my nature— that is, they have my own power (prabhāva) within them;
they were born from the mere volition of my very mind, which is Hiraṇyagarbha in essence.
He speaks of their power with the words "of whom":

of those such as Bhṛgu and others, Sanaka and others, and the Manus, these offspring—consisting of sons, grandsons, and so forth, as well as disciples and grand-disciples, beginning with Brāhmaṇas and others—have been born and continue to increase in the world according to their respective natures. //6//
Madhusūdana:
And for this very reason, O great sages (*maharṣayaḥ*).

The "great sages" are those who have seen the Vedas and their meaning—the omniscient ones such as Bhṛgu and others, the seven ancient seers (*sapta pūrve*) who appeared at the beginning of creation and were the originators of the tradition of knowledge.
And likewise, in the Purāṇa:
"The one of great splendor created by his mind these sons: Bhṛgu, Marīci, Atri, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu, and Vasiṣṭha."
"These seven are known as the Brahmās; such is the certainty established in the Purāṇas" (Mbh 12.201.4–5).
Likewise, there are the four Manūs known as the Sāvarṇas;
or else, the seven great Ṛṣis beginning with Bhṛgu.

Even prior to them were the first four great sages, Sanaka and the others, as well as the fourteen Manus, beginning with Svāyambhuva; those whose disposition (*bhāva*)—that is, their contemplation (*bhāvanā*)—was directed toward Me, the Supreme Lord, were "possessed of My disposition" (*mad-bhāvāḥ*), meaning they were intent on meditating upon Me, and by virtue of that meditation, the powers of My knowledge and sovereignty became manifest within them. This is the sense.
The *mānasas* were born solely from the mental resolve (*saṅkalpa*) of the Mind (*manas*), and not from a womb;

therefore, by virtue of their pure birth, they are the best among all living beings. They were born from me alone—having manifested at the beginning of creation from my own self as Hiraṇyagarbha. From these seven great seers (*maharṣis*) such as Bhṛgu and others, the four [sages] such as Sanaka and others, and the fourteen Manus, have descended these lineages consisting of Brāhmaṇas and the other castes in this world, both through birth and through learning.
All creatures. //6//
Viśvanātha:

Having mentioned those who are incapable of knowing their own true nature due to delusion regarding intellect and knowledge, he now speaks of those who are likewise incapable even of that [true nature].
The seven great seers (maharṣis) beginning with Marīci, and prior to them, the four others beginning with Sanaka, are the Manus.
The fourteen [sages] beginning with Svāyambhuva, whose birth (bhava) originated from me alone in the form of Hiraṇyagarbha—

namely Marīci and others, as well as Sanaka and others— their progeny (prajā) existing in this world in the form of sons, grandsons, and so forth, as well as in the form of disciples and grand-disciples, consist of these [beings] beginning with the Brāhmaṇas. //6//
Baladeva says: "And for this very reason, it is so," as stated in the verse beginning with "the great sages" (*maharṣayaḥ*).
These seven, headed by Bhṛgu; those even prior to them, the first four, Sanaka and the others; these eleven great sages (*maharṣis*);
likewise, the fourteen Manus, beginning with Svāyambhuva—these twenty-five are the mind-born (*mānasa*) offspring of Hiraṇyagarbha.

The meaning is that those [beings], beginning with my mind, were born from me; their disposition is toward me, they are intent on meditating upon me, and by my power they have attained the capacities of my knowledge and sovereignty.
From these twenty-five, such as Bhṛgu and others, these offspring—consisting of Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and so forth—are produced in the form of a lineage through both birth and learning. //6//
He who knows this majesty and this yoga of Mine in its true essence is united with unshakable yoga; of this there is no doubt. (10.7)

Śrīdhara: He states the fruit of the knowledge of the reality of the aforementioned manifestations and so forth with the words "this" (etām). This refers to my manifestation characterized by Bhṛgu and others, as well as to yoga characterized by sovereign power (aiśvarya).
He who knows this in reality becomes endowed with non-conceptual, doubt-free yoga—that is, with right vision; there is no doubt about this. //7//
Madhusūdana:
Having thus described the power of the Lord as possessed of limiting adjuncts (*sopādhika*), he speaks of the fruit of knowing that [power] with the words "etām" (this).

This refers to the aforementioned manifestation (*vibhūti*)—consisting of forms such as the intellect (*buddhi*) and the great seers (*maharṣi*), etc.—which is a manifold state (*vividha-bhāva*) existing in various respective forms; and "yoga," which is the capacity for creative manifestation (*nirmāṇa-sāmarthya*) for those respective purposes, [and] supreme sovereignty (*paramaiśvarya*).
Thus it is said:

he who knows me as I truly am, in accordance with reality, is joined with yoga—that is, with meditative absorption (*samādhi*) characterized by the stability of right knowledge—which is unshakable and immovable; of this there is no doubt, nor is there any obstacle whatsoever. //7//
Viśvanātha:

However, because of my statement, "But by singular devotion alone am I to be grasped" (BhP 11.14.11), it is only my exclusive devotee who, through my grace, maintains firm faith in my words and knows my true nature; thus he says this in brief.
He who knows in truth the majesty and yoga—that is, the yoga of devotion—to be described hereafter;

he who, because these words are from My Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa, possesses a most firm conviction that "this alone is the supreme reality"; such a person is joined, indeed becomes united, with unwavering and steady yoga characterized by the knowledge of My true nature. Of this there is no doubt whatsoever. //7//
Baladeva: He states the fruit of knowing the meaning thus explained with the words "etām" (this).

This refers to the manifestation characterized by supreme sovereignty, namely that the entire phenomenal world—including the deities such as Brahmā and Rudra, the great sages such as Sanaka and others, and the Manus headed by Svāyambhuva—exists and functions with its knowledge and power of lordship dependent upon Me. Thus [he describes] this manifestation characterized by supreme sovereignty.

He who knows that this yoga— consisting of my connection with the jewels of auspicious qualities such as beginninglessness and birthlessness— is taught by Vāsudeva, the Lord of all and the Omniscient One, and who accepts it with firm conviction that "this is the essential truth," becomes endowed with, or perfected in, the unwavering and steady yoga characterized by devotion to Me.
The meaning is that, by being of such a nature, my knowledge generates and increases devotion to me. //7//
I am the source of all; from me everything emanates.
Realizing this, the wise, filled with devotion, worship me. (10.8)

Śrīdhara: He demonstrates how the attainment of perfect knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*) occurs through the knowledge of the manifestations (*vibhūti*) and yoga by means of the four verses beginning with "I am" (*aham*).

"I am the source of the entire world"—that is, the cause of its origin by way of manifestations such as Bhṛgu and the Manus. And from Me alone proceed everything, including the intellect, knowledge, and the absence of delusion of the whole world.
Thinking thus and having realized this, the wise, who possess discrimination and are endowed with devotion, worship me with love. //8//
Madhusūdana:
By means of the four verses beginning with "I am," He shows by what kind of knowledge of *vibhūti* (manifest power) and *yoga* (union) the attainment of unshakable *yoga* occurs.

"I" refers to the Supreme Brahman known as Vāsudeva, the source—the cause of the origin, both material (*upādāna*) and efficient (*nimitta*)—of the entire world; the maintenance, destruction, and so forth of everything proceed from Me alone.
[It] exists; impelled by Me alone—the inner controller (*antaryāmin*), the omniscient, and omnipotent—all the world proceeds or exerts itself without transgressing its respective boundaries.
Thinking thus, the wise, endowed with love that consists in grasping the ultimate reality through discrimination and the realization of the true nature of things, worship Me. //8//
Viśvanātha:

Regarding that, he describes His manifestation characterized by supreme sovereignty: "I am the source—the cause of both the origination and the appearance—of everything consisting of all material and non-material objects. From Me alone, in My form as the Inner Controller, the entire universe proceeds and acts."

Likewise, from Me alone—manifesting as incarnations such as Nārada and others—all means of practice, such as devotion, knowledge, austerity, and ritual action, as well as their respective results, have proceeded. Thinking thus, [the Lord] spoke of yoga characterized by exclusive devotion; the meaning is that He did so having ascertained this through knowledge born of faith (*āstikya*).
"Those endowed with *bhāva*" refers to those possessed of the moods of servitude, friendship, and so forth. //8//

Baladeva: Now, speaking of the devotion of the supreme devotees (*paramaikāntinaḥ*) through these four verses, he first describes the true nature of the Self, which is both the progenitor and the nourisher of that devotion, beginning with the words "I am.

I, Kṛṣṇa, the Blessed Lord Himself, am the source—the cause—of this entire phenomenal world (*prapañca*), headed by Brahmā and Rudra. Thus it is recited in the Atharvaveda: "He who in the beginning created Brahmā, and who indeed caused the Vedas to be sung, He is Kṛṣṇa" (GTU 1.22).
Then, beginning with "Now, indeed, the Person Nārāyaṇa desired: 'May I create offspring,'" [it continues]: "From Nārāyaṇa Brahmā is born;
from Nārāyaṇa Prajāpati is born; from Nārāyaṇa Indra is born; from Nārāyaṇa the eight Vasus are born;
from Nārāyaṇa the eleven Rudras are born; from Nārāyaṇa the twelve Ādityas [are born]," and so forth.
"This Kṛṣṇa, the son of Devakī, who is devoted to Brahman, is to be understood as Nārāyaṇa," according to the subsequent reading beginning with these words.

Regarding this, they say: "In the beginning, there was indeed only Nārāyaṇa; there was no Brahmā, no Īśāna, no waters, no serpents, nor were these two, heaven and earth, nor the stars, nor the sun. He, being alone, did not delight; while he remained absorbed in meditation..."

In this [text], beginning with the words "Where the Chāndogyas, performing the rites known as Aṣṭakā and others, speak of the Stoma," and after describing the creation of Pradhāna and the rest, it is further stated: "Then Nārāyaṇa, desiring something else, meditated with his mind;
from him, while thus absorbed in meditation, there was born from his forehead a three-eyed, trident-handed person, bearing splendor."
"Truth, celibacy, austerity, and dispassion"—and [the statement] "therein one is born with four faces," and so forth;
and in the *Ṛgveda* verses: "Whomever I desire, him I make fierce; him I make a Brahmin, him a seer, him wise," and so forth.
And in the Mokṣadharma:
"I indeed create both Prajāpati and Rudra;
for they, deluded by my māyā, recognize me [as their creator]. Thus it is said.
And in the Vārāha [Purāṇa]: "Nārāyaṇa is the supreme deity; from him was born the four-faced [Brahmā];
from him the god Rudra came into being, and he attained omniscience. Thus it is said.
It has been stated that "I am the sole controller of everything other than myself.
Thinking thus and ascertaining my such nature from the mouth of a true guru, the wise, endowed with devotion—that is, love—worship me. //8//
With their minds fixed on me and their lives surrendered to me, enlightening one another and constantly speaking of me, they find contentment and delight. (10.9)
Śrīdhara: He speaks of worship preceded by love with the words "mac-cittāḥ" (those whose minds are fixed on Me).
Those whose consciousness (*citta*) is directed toward Me alone are "mac-cittāḥ.
Those whose vital breaths (*prāṇa*), meaning their senses (*indriya*), have gone to and reached Me alone are "mad-gata-prāṇāḥ."
Or, [the phrase] may mean "those whose lives are dedicated to me.

Being such as these, those wise ones, mutually enlightening one another regarding Me through the means of valid knowledge such as the Vedas which are endowed with reason, and describing Me through their intellect while chanting My names, being virtuous, they are eternally satisfied;
that is, they attain satisfaction through sympathetic rejoicing (anumodana).
They delight and attain liberation. //9//
Madhusūdana explains that worship preceded by love alone is what is intended by the words "mac-cittāḥ":
those whose minds are fixed on Me, the Blessed Lord, are "mac-cittāḥ."

Likewise, "those whose life-breaths have gone to Me" (mad-gata-prāṇāḥ) refers to those whose vital functions, such as sight and so forth, have reached Me; that is, their activities of the eyes and other senses are directed toward My worship, or else all their faculties have been withdrawn into Me. Alternatively, "those whose life-breaths have gone to Me" means those whose very existence is for the sake of worshipping Me—that is to say, their lives are devoid of any purpose other than My worship.

In assemblies of the learned, they mutually awaken one another regarding Me alone through scriptural citations and logical arguments, making it known through discourse with those desiring to know the truth;
likewise, they speak of Me alone and instruct their own disciples.
Thus, among equals, there is the offering of the mind to Me, as well as the offering of the external senses and the offering of one’s very life.
They are satisfied by that very form of devotion to Me which consists of awakening others to Me and instructing those who are inferior to themselves;
they attain contentment in the form of the conviction: "We have obtained all our goals through this alone; we have no need for anything else that remains to be attained."
By means of that contentment, they rejoice and delight, and they experience supreme happiness as if through union with a beloved.
As it was said by Patañjali: "From contentment comes the attainment of unsurpassed happiness" (Yogasūtra 2.42).
And it is said in the Purāṇa:

Whatever sensual pleasure there is in the world, and whatever great divine pleasure there is—these are not worth even a sixteenth part of the happiness that comes from the destruction of craving. Thus it is said.
The destruction of craving is contentment. //9//
Viśvanātha:

It is precisely such exclusive devotees who, having attained the yoga of intelligence through My grace, obtain the knowledge of My true nature—which, as previously described, is difficult to comprehend—even though it is hard to understand. He says this: "Those whose minds are fixed on Me, their hearts greedy only for the tasting of the sweetness of My form, names, qualities, and pastimes..."

With their life-breaths fixed on Me—just as men whose life-breaths are fixed on food are unable to sustain their lives without it—they awaken [others] by making known the nature, modes, and other aspects of devotion through their affection;

they speak of Me, the great ocean of most sweet forms, qualities, and pastimes, and perform recitation and other acts by explaining My form and so forth. Thus, because of its preeminence among all forms of devotion, remembrance, hearing, and recitation [are the best].
It has been said that "they are satisfied and they rejoice"; the secret meaning is that through devotion alone there is both satisfaction and delight.
Alternatively, even during the stage of spiritual practice (*sādhana*), when the act of worship is accomplished without obstacles by the power of fortune, they are satisfied.

At that very moment, by recollecting their own future state of accomplishment, they rejoice; and because they rejoice with their Lord in their minds, devotion characterized by the path of passion (rāgānugā-bhakti) is thus illustrated. //9//

Baladeva explains the manner of devotion with the words "mac-cittā" (those whose minds are fixed on Me): those whose minds are fixed on Me, who are intent on remembering Me, whose life-breaths are dedicated to Me— unable to sustain their lives without Me, like fish without water—
and who mutually awaken one another to My form, qualities, beauty, and so forth, as well as to Me, the ocean of affection for My own devotees.
Narrating His most diverse deeds, they thus find satisfaction through the modes of worship characterized by remembrance, hearing, and chanting— as if drinking nectar—
and likewise they delight in those very things, such as the smiles and sidelong glances of young women.
"They are satisfied and they rejoice"—this is the secret: that through devotion alone there is both satisfaction and rejoicing.
Alternatively, even during the stage of practice (*sādhana-daśā*), when worship is accomplished without obstacle by the power of good fortune, they are satisfied;
and at that very moment, recollecting their own future state of attainment (*sādhya-daśā*), they rejoice in their minds together with their Lord. Thus, *rāgānugā* devotion is illuminated. //9//
To those who are constantly disciplined and who worship Me with love, I grant that yoga of discernment by which they come to Me. (10)
Śrīdhara: And He says, "I grant perfect knowledge to those who have become such," with the words "to them" (teṣām).

To those who are thus constantly disciplined, whose minds are attached to Me, and who worship Me with love—I grant that yoga which is the means consisting of wisdom. What is that? It is the means by which those devotees of Mine attain Me. //10//
Madhusūdana says: "Of those who worship Me in the manner described"— that is,
of those who are constantly, at all times, disciplined, with their intellects one-pointedly fixed on the Blessed Lord.

Therefore, for those who worship and serve Me with joy alone, without aiming for gain, honor, fame, or the like—I grant, that is, I produce, that very "discriminative yoga" (buddhi-yoga) concerning Me, the Self, which was previously described as being attained through unwavering yoga; by means of which discriminative yoga they come to Me, the Lord, as their own Self, they who worship Me in such ways as by fixing the mind on Me. 10.
Viśvanātha:

Now, from your statement that "they are satisfied and they rejoice," it is understood that for your devotees, supreme bliss—which transcends all qualities—is attained through devotion alone; however, what is the method for their direct attainment of You?
In response to the inquiry as to from whom that [knowledge] must be understood by them, He says: "To them" (teṣām).
To those who are "ever-devoted"—meaning those who constantly long for union with Me—I grant that yoga of wisdom; I alone manifest it within their mental faculties.
The sense is this: that yoga of wisdom cannot be attained either by itself or from any other source whatsoever, but is to be given by Me alone and received by them alone.
They come to me, they perceive me, and they reach my immediate presence. //10//

Baladeva: If it be asked, "How can they be able to grasp You, who are infinite in Your essential nature, attributes, and manifestations, merely through the instruction of a teacher? he says in response, "Of them" (teṣām).

To those who are constantly disciplined (*satata-yuktānām*), who always desire union with Me, and who worship Me with love—possessing an abundance of relish born from the knowledge of My true nature—I, who am a connoisseur of the rasa of their devotion, bestow that yoga of the intellect (*buddhi-yogam*) and grant it to them.
I manifest that very understanding by which they approach Me, so that, having grasped Me as one whose power and qualities are infinite and having worshipped Me, they attain Me. //10//
Out of compassion for them alone, I, dwelling within their very self, destroy the darkness born of ignorance with the shining lamp of knowledge. (11)

Śrīdhara: Having bestowed the yoga of wisdom upon them and having revealed it until its culmination in direct experience, He says "of them" (teṣām), meaning: "For the sake of compassion—that is, for the sake of favor—I destroy the darkness born of ignorance, which is called saṃsāra. Abiding where, or by what means, do You destroy that darkness?
Therefore he says: "Abiding in the self-nature, remaining established in the function of the intellect, I destroy [it] by means of the shining, radiant lamp characterized by knowledge. (11)
Madhusūdana:

Regarding the fruit of the yoga of discernment (*buddhi-yoga*) being bestowed for the attainment of the Self, [the Lord] states the intermediate operation in the words "of them" (*teṣām*). For the sake of favoring them so that their own welfare may be realized, [He acts] within the modification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa-vṛtti*) which takes the form of the Self (*ātmākāra*), [which is the state of] His own nature (*ātmabhāva*).

I, the Self, abiding as the object [of knowledge], characterized by self-luminous consciousness and non-dual bliss, dispel— by means of that very light of knowledge which is a transformation of my own internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa),
resembling a lamp, radiant, endowed with the reflection of consciousness (cid-ābhāsa), and unobstructed— the darkness born of ignorance,

having ignorance as its material cause, characterized by false cognition, obscuring its own object, and consisting of gloom; this is done through the destruction of the ignorance that serves as its material cause.

I destroy [it], because ignorance, which is the material cause of all delusion, is removable by knowledge, and because that which is derived from a material cause is removed by the destruction of that cause.

Just as when darkness is to be dispelled by a lamp, there is no dependence on ritual action or practice other than the arising of the lamp; and since it is the manifestation of an already existing thing, nothing that has not arisen comes into being—so it is here.
Since ignorance is to be removed by knowledge, there is no dependence on any other action or practice apart from the arising of knowledge;

and since liberation, which is the very nature of Brahman already existing, is its manifestation, it is not something unarisen that must arise—by which it would be subject to decay or dependence on action and the like. This is the meaning indicated through the figure of speech known as *rūpaka* (metaphorical identification).
By the word "bhāsvatā" (by the luminous one), the absence of obstacles—such as intense winds and so forth—is indicated, just as [the absence of] disbelief and so forth [is an obstacle to knowledge].

Furthermore, the similarity between knowledge and a lamp should be understood as the basis for the metaphor (*rūpaka*): namely, that [knowledge] removes the obscuration of its own object, that it does not depend on another of its own kind for its own empirical usage (*vyavahāra*), and that it does not depend on any auxiliary cause other than its own production, and so on. //11//
Viśvanātha:
But surely, how can there be the attainment of You without the practice of knowledge and so forth?
Therefore, one must certainly strive for that purpose by means of those [practices] as well.

In this regard, he says "not at all, not at all" for the sake of compassion toward them—meaning, for the sake of that manner in which my compassion toward them may arise—and not for the sake of other yogis.
The sense is that they need have no concern whatsoever regarding the attainment of my compassion, because I myself am already striving for the purpose of their attaining my compassion;
for I abide within their very being, established in the functioning of their intellect.

Because that knowledge is illuminated by Me alone, it is not merely *sāttvika*; even though it is devoid of the material qualities (*nirguṇa*), it is distinct from the knowledge arising from devotion (*bhakti*). Since I am the very lamp by which that [knowledge] exists, how could they strive for its sake?

For I have declared, "I carry the acquisition and preservation (*yoga-kṣema*) of those who are constantly devoted" (Gītā 9.22); thus, I have accepted to bear all their burdens, both worldly and ultimate.
Such is the meaning.
The illustrious Gītā, which is the essence of all, removes the distress of living beings; this four-verse summary has been proclaimed, renowned for bestowing peace upon all. (11)
Baladeva: If it is asked, "Since the darkness of ignorance has existed for a long time, how can there be the manifestation of that [light] in their hearts? he says in response, "Of them alone.

This refers only to those who are exclusively devoted to me (*mad-ekāntinaḥ*) and are unable to sustain their lives without me—not, however, to those established in other systems—for the sake of compassion, meaning for the sake of making them worthy recipients of my grace.
Remaining within my own self, like a bee within the calyx of a lotus, I abide in that state manifesting my divine form and qualities;

by means of the shining lamp of knowledge regarding them, I destroy the darkness consisting of the longing for objects other than Me, which is born of beginningless ignorance in the form of karma that opposes knowledge.

"Being propitiated by their single-minded devotion, I shall effect the manifestation of the state of consciousness characterized by security (yoga-kṣema) and the destruction of the darkness residing therein; since the burden of sustaining all that belongs to me alone, they need not exert themselves for any purpose whatsoever"—thus it was said. This is what has been proclaimed in these two [chapters] beginning with the ninth, which form the core of the Gītā.
That alone is the essence of the meaning of the Gītā scripture; it should be understood by the wise. //11//
Arjuna said:
You are the Supreme Brahman, the Supreme Abode, and the Highest Purifier.
The eternal, divine Person, the primordial God, unborn and all-pervading.
"All the sages, as well as the celestial sage Nārada, Asita, Devala, and Vyāsa, have said this of you; and you yourself tell it to me. (13)

Śrīdhara: Desiring to know in detail the majesty (vibhūti) that has been briefly described, Arjuna, praising the Blessed One, spoke with seven verses beginning with "The Supreme Brahman. You alone are the Supreme Abode (paraṃ dhāma), the Refuge (āśrayaḥ), and the Supreme Purifier (paramaṃ pavitram).
Why is this? To this he says: because [he is] the eternal, constant Person;
likewise, the divine, whose nature is luminosity and who is self-effulgent;
and he is both the beginning and the God—therefore, him.
The meaning is that he is the primordial source of the gods; likewise, he is unborn (*aja*), being without birth,
and all-pervading (*vibhu*).
"They say it is you alone.
"Who are they? he asks. He says, "They say," meaning all the sages, such as Bhṛgu and others.
And the celestial sage Nārada, Asita, Devala, Vyāsa, and you yourself—directly to me, you speak [of this]. //12-13//
Madhusūdana:
Having thus heard of the Lord’s majesty and yoga, Arjuna, filled with supreme longing, spoke in seven verses beginning with "the Supreme Brahman.
"The Supreme Brahman" refers to the highest reality, the supreme abode, the refuge, or the light.
You alone are the supreme purifier and sanctifier,

because you are the Person, the Supreme Self, eternal, always of one form, divine— existing in the highest heaven within your own essential nature— and the primordial cause of all, the Lord whose nature is luminosity and who is self-effulgent, transcending your own phenomenal expansion.
The syntactical connection is: "Therefore, they call You the primordial God, the unborn, the all-pervading, and the omnipresent. //12//
All the sages, such as Bhṛgu and Vasiṣṭha, who are established in the knowledge of reality, speak of you and declare that your greatness is infinite;
likewise do the celestial sage Nārada, Asita Devala, Dhaumya’s elder brother,
and the venerable Vyāsa Kṛṣṇa-Dvaipāyana.
These [sages] also spoke to me directly about you, who possess the previously mentioned attributes; what need is there for other speakers, since you yourself speak to me?
Here, although they are sages, Nārada and others are mentioned separately because they are exceptionally distinguished as direct speakers. (13)
Viśvanātha:
Desiring to hear in detail the meaning that was stated in brief, he speaks preceded by praise, beginning with the word "param" (supreme).
The supreme abode (*dhāma*), Śyāmasundara—the dark and beautiful form—is indeed the Supreme Brahman.
According to Amara, "abodes" (dhāmāni) refers to houses, bodies, splendor, and powers;
you are indeed such an abode.
The sense is that, like the individual soul (jīva), there is no distinction between your body and your self.
Of what nature is that abode?

It is supremely pure, removing the impurity of ignorance from those who behold it; therefore, even the seers call You the eternal Person (*puruṣa*), declaring the permanence of this form of a person. (12–13)
Baladeva: Desiring to hear in detail the manifestation of power that he has heard only in brief, Arjuna said, "The Supreme.
You alone are the Supreme Brahman, as it is heard in scripture: "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite.
You alone are the Supreme Abode, the reality that is the support of all, as it is heard in scripture: "All things rest in That; no one transcends It. You are that very thing.

"I know that very object which removes all the sins of the one who remembers it—of which it is heard in scripture: 'Only you, O Lord, knowing the Supreme Purifier, are liberated from all sins; you cross over every evil, and no evil crosses over you,' and so forth. Likewise, all the sages favored by Him, and among them the foremost such as Nārada and others [have declared this]. Therefore, Kṛṣṇa alone is the Supreme God; one should meditate upon Him, taste Him, worship Him, and sacrifice to Him."
Thus:

"Oṃ tat sat"— those who know the meaning of the Śruti declare you to be this divine Puruṣa, the primordial God, unborn and all-pervading, distinct from birth and old age, an immovable pillar, and indestructible (Gītā 2.22).

10.12] You yourself declare this in conversations concerning those [teachings], in the Purāṇas, and in the Itihāsas, through such statements as: "Though I am unborn and my nature is imperishable" (Gītā 4.6), "He who knows me as unborn and beginningless" (Gītā 10.3), and "I am the source of all" (Gītā 10.8), and so forth. //12-13//
O Keśava, I consider all this that you tell me to be the truth;
for neither the gods nor the demons, O Blessed One, know your manifestation.
Śrīdhara: Therefore, he says "all this" (*sarvam etat*) to indicate that his own disbelief regarding Your sovereignty has now ceased.
Through this realization—that You are the Supreme Brahman and so forth—I consider all of it to be *ṛtam*, meaning true;
namely, what You have told me, beginning with "The hosts of gods do not know Me," and so on.
"I consider even that to be truly so," he says with the words "for not" (na hi).
O Blessed One, the gods do not know your manifestation;
they do not realize that this manifestation is for the sake of showing favor to us.
And the Dānavas did not even realize that he was there for the purpose of their subjugation. //14//
Madhusūdana:

All this that has been spoken by the sages and by you is indeed true; I consider it to be exactly so, O Keśava, regarding what you say to me. For there is no suspicion whatsoever of invalidity in your words.

And because You know that through Your omniscience, the term *keśava*—derived from the etymology "he who understands even Keśa and Śava (Brahmā and Rudra), though they are the lords of all, by means of compassion"—indicates Your unsurpassed sovereignty.
Therefore, what was stated [in the Gītā]: "Neither the hosts of gods nor the great seers know My origin" (10.2), and so forth, is indeed exactly so.

For indeed, O Blessed One, endowed with complete sovereignty and all other perfections, even the gods—who possess superior knowledge—do not know Your manifestation or power; nor do the Dānavas, nor the great sages. This is also to be understood as stated by Viśvanātha.
"I have no lack of faith in this matter," he says with the word "all.
Furthermore, those sages call you, the unborn, the supreme abode of Brahman;
they do not know of your manifestation as birth.
The meaning is that they do not know in what manner both your state of being unborn and your state of possessing birth belong to you, whose nature is the Supreme Brahman.
Therefore, O Keśava, I consider everything that You have said— "Neither the hosts of gods nor the great seers know My origin" (Gītā 10.2)— to be entirely true and real.

The meaning is this: since you bind even Brahmā, Īśa, and Rudra—who are themselves of such age—through their ignorance of their own true nature, what need is there to mention that the gods, dānavas, and others do not know you? Thus it should be said. //14//
Baladeva: "All this"—
I consider all this to be indeed *ṛta* and *satya*, and not merely a matter of praise.
"O Keśava!"—you who, by binding both Vidhi and Rudra through ignorance of their own true nature, bind Prajāpati and Rudra as well; thus you have been described. O Lord of All!
O Blessed One, O treasury of the six sovereign powers of limitless excellence!

The meaning is this: even the gods and demons do not recognize Your glorious form, which manifests qualities such as being the Supreme Brahman; for they disregard You and act with malice toward You, perceiving You as belonging to their own or another [inferior] class.
O Supreme Person, O Creator of beings, O Lord of beings, O God of gods, O Master of the world, You alone know Yourself by Yourself. (10.15)
Śrīdhara: What then? "By yourself. You alone know—that is, you understand—yourself; no one else does.
And even that [knowledge of yourself], you know by means of your very own self.
Not by any other means of proof.
He addresses him with great reverence in many ways: "O Puruṣottama!
These vocatives are epithets that contain within them the reasons for his being the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama).
O creator of beings, O progenitor of beings;
O Lord of beings, O controller;
O God of gods, such as Āditya and others, O illuminator.
O Lord of the world, O Protector of the universe! //15//
Madhusūdana:
Since you are the beginning of all of them and your knowledge is impossible [to attain], therefore [the Lord says] "by yourself.
That is, by yourself alone—without even mutual instruction and so forth—you yourself, by your own nature, [know] yourself both in its unconditioned (nirupādhika) and conditioned (sopādhika) aspects.

"You alone know [Me]—as the unconditioned through the state of being the inner self (pratyaktva) beyond the reach of the senses, and as the conditioned through the possession of unsurpassed powers such as knowledge and sovereignty;

no one else knows Me. Dispelling the doubt, 'How could I know You who cannot be known by others?', You address Me in many ways out of affection and longing: 'O Puruṣottama! Compared to You, all other persons are indeed inferior.'"
Therefore, the intention is that what is impossible for them is indeed possible for You, the Supreme One.
He further elucidates Your status as the Supreme Person through four vocatives:
"O Bhūtabhāvana," meaning You who nourish—that is, bring forth—all beings; O Father of all beings.

Even a father is not always desired [as a refuge]; therefore he says: "O Lord of Beings (bhūteśa)," meaning the controller of all beings. Even a controller is not always worthy of worship; therefore he says: "O God of Gods (devadeva)," meaning the one to be worshipped even by the gods who are themselves worthy of worship by all.

Even one worthy of worship is not necessarily a protector as a lord; therefore he says: "O Lord of the World (jagatpate)," meaning the protector of the entire world by virtue of being the author of the Vedas which instruct on what is beneficial and harmful.

Being distinguished by all such attributes, you are the father of all, the teacher of all, and the king of all; therefore, O Supreme Person (Puruṣottama), what more need be said? You are to be propitiated by everyone in every way—this is the intended meaning. //15//
Viśvanātha:

Therefore, you alone know yourself; by the word "alone" (eva), the meaning is that even though your lack of crookedness, your being born, and so forth are difficult to reconcile, your devotee knows them as indeed real, yet even he does not know by what manner [those qualities exist].
You know that as well by yourself alone, not by any other means;
for this very reason, you are the most excellent among men, even in the midst of the great creators and others.
You are not merely the most excellent, however.
Because he is the creator of the elements (*bhūta-bhāvana*);
he is the Lord (*īśa*) of those beings who consist of the nature of elemental creation, beginning with them and ending with Parameṣṭhin.
He is not merely a lord alone; [he is the source].
The meaning is that since those gods are the very ones by whom You play—meaning they have become the instruments of Your sport—they exist solely for the purpose of Your play.
Furthermore, the meaning of the four vocative phrases is: "Out of the power of Your boundless compassion, You alone become the Lord even for those like me who dwell in the world.
Alternatively, it explains Your very status as the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama): "O Bhūtabhāvana, O Father of all beings!"
"Is there no one even who is not desired as a father?
To that he says: "O Lord of Beings" (bhūteśa). "Is there no one even who is not to be propitiated? To that he says: "O God of Gods" (devadeva).
To this he replies: "O Lord of the World," [implying] that even one who is to be propitiated by the gods does not protect [us]. //15//

Baladeva: You yourself, by your own self and by your own knowledge, fully know yourself—that you are "this" and "thus. Those among the gods and the Dānavas who are your devotees certainly know your form as a real entity; since they know it to be such, how could they not know it? This is indicated by the emphatic particle *eva*. O Puruṣottama, Lord of all beings!
Being the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama), You awaken [me] by revealing Yourself, O Creator of Beings (bhūtabhāvana)!
O progenitor of all living creatures! Even though one might be a creator of beings, such a person is not desired [by me].

To that he says: "O Lord of Beings (bhūteśa)," meaning the controller of all living creatures. [An objector might say: even the Lord of Beings is not worthy of worship by someone; to that he replies: "O God of Gods (devadeva)."
Even after propitiating all the gods who are to be worshipped, there is no protector there, even for a god among gods; thus he said: "O Lord of the World!
O Protector of the Universe! [You are the one] through instruction in what is beneficial and harmful, and by surrendering my livelihood."
For one such as you, reality is perfectly established. //15//
You ought to describe without omission Your divine self-manifestations, by which manifestations You abide pervading these worlds. (16)
Śrīdhara: Since you alone know your own manifestation and not the gods and others, therefore [it is said] "to speak.
You alone are worthy—that is, capable—of speaking of all those divine and most wonderful manifestations of yours, the Self.
The phrase "by which" is an adjective qualifying the manifestations (*vibhūtayaḥ*), intended for clarity. //16//
Madhusūdana:
Since your manifestations (*vibhūtayaḥ*) are impossible for all others to know and must necessarily be known by you, therefore [I shall] speak of them.
Those manifestations by which you abide pervading all these worlds—those are your uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*) manifestations.
Since these divine [matters] cannot be known by those who are not omniscient, you alone, being omniscient, ought to explain them in their entirety. //16//
Viśvanātha:

Illuminating the fact that while Your true nature is difficult to fathom, my desire arises specifically for Your manifestations (*vibhūti*), He says, "to speak. The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is: "You ought to speak, first of all, those divine—that is, supreme—manifestations of the Self."
Now, one might object that it is indeed impossible to describe all my manifestations in their entirety; to this he replies with the words "by which... (verse 16).

Baladeva: Indeed, since the true nature of Your essence is thus so difficult to fathom, my desire for knowledge arises specifically regarding Your manifestations (vibhūtis). Indicating this, He says, "to speak" (vaktum).
You ought to speak exhaustively of Your divine and supreme manifestations, which are unique to Yourself; here the nominative case is used in the sense of the accusative.
It is by means of these [manifestations] that You, distinguished [by them], remain pervading and governing these worlds. //16//
O Yogi, how may I know You by constantly meditating upon You? And in what various manifestations, O Blessed One, are You to be contemplated by me? (10.17)
Śrīdhara: Showing the purpose of the discourse, he makes this request with two verses beginning with "How" (katham).

O Yogin, by what various manifestations (vibhūti-bheda) should I know You, always contemplating You? Even though You are to be contemplated through Your various manifestations, in which specific objects am I to contemplate You? //17//
Madhusūdana:
What is the purpose of explaining that? He states it with two verses beginning with "How" (*katham*).
*Yoga* is the power of unsurpassed sovereignty and so forth; since he possesses this, O *yogin*, you who are endowed with the power of unsurpassed sovereignty and so forth.

I am of exceedingly dull intellect; how could I know You, who are impossible even for the gods and others to know, though I should constantly reflect upon and meditate on You? [Objection: "Surely by meditating on Me within My manifestations (vibhūtis), you will come to know Me. To this He replies: "In which and which entities—among all things, both sentient and insentient, that have become Your manifestations—am I to be meditated upon by me, O Blessed One?"

Viśvanātha: O Yogin, how may I, while constantly reflecting upon You— who possess the power of Yoga and Yoga-māyā— come to know You as the Eternal Wisdom (Sadā-vidyā), just as one might reflect upon the one wearing a forest garland (Vanamālī)?
This is because of your statement: "Through devotion he comes to know me in truth, as who I am and what I am" (BhP 11.14.11).
Likewise, the meaning is: "In which states or objects (*bhāva-padārtha*) are you to be contemplated? Devotion consisting of contemplation of you is to be performed by me. //17//
Baladeva said: "Indeed, for what purpose is that being described? To this he replies with the word 'how' (katham).
O Yogi—meaning, one who possesses the power of *yoga-māyā*—how shall I know [perceive] You, the possessor of infinite auspicious qualities, by constantly contemplating and remembering You?"
In which states and in which objects, manifesting as You, am I to contemplate and meditate upon You?
Tell me both of these;
the meaning is that since this will be accomplished by way of an enumeration of Your manifestations, please teach them. //17//
O Janārdana, tell me again in detail of Your own yoga and majesty; for there is no satiety for me as I listen to this nectar. 18.

Śrīdhara: Thus, although [Arjuna] is outward-looking, Śrī Kṛṣṇa speaks at length so that his mind may remain fixed on Him alone through various manifestations of His glory; hence He says, "speak at length.
Speak again in detail of Your own yoga—Your sovereign power characterized by omniscience, omnipotence, and so forth—and Your vibhūtis (manifestations).
For as I listen to Your words, which are like nectar, my intellect finds no satiety. (18)
Madhusūdana:
Therefore, [the Lord says] "in detail":
[tell me] of your own *yoga*, characterized by omniscience, omnipotence, and so forth—your supreme sovereignty and *vibhūti* (manifestation).

And the object of meditation has been explained in detail and in brief in the seventh and ninth chapters; yet, O Janārdana, please speak further, for you are entreated by all people regarding the purpose of worldly prosperity and the supreme good.
Therefore, my request to you is indeed appropriate.

To the question, "Why do you ask again what has already been said? he replies: "Satiety does not exist through the notion of 'enough,' for there is no cessation of desire for one who hears [you], drinking your words like nectar—sweet, as it were, at every step."

Since the phrase "your words" is not explicitly stated here, this is a fusion (*saṅkara*) of the figures of speech *apahnuti* (concealment), *atiśayokti* (hyperbole), and *rūpaka* (metaphor); it manifests an intensity of longing through the experience of an excellence of sweetness. //18//
Viśvanātha:

By the very statement, "I am the source of all; from me everything proceeds" (Gītā 10.8), it has already been taught that all objects are my manifestations (*vibhūti*) and that those very manifestations spoken of by me are indeed such; thus, thinking in this way, they worship me—this is precisely what is called *bhakti-yoga*.

Regarding this, he says "in detail": "O Janārdana!"—the sense is: "By the sweetness of your beneficial instruction, you alone arouse desire in people like me and thus afflict us by making us beg; what can we do?
[This is said] by one who hears the nectar of your instruction and tastes it with the tongue of the ears. //18//

Baladeva: If it is argued, "But has not the connection with auspicious qualities such as being unborn already been stated repeatedly in previous passages beginning with *ajo 'pi san* (Gītā 4.6), and have His manifestations not also been stated in passages beginning with *raso 'ham* (Gītā 7.8)? Why then do you ask again?"—to that he replies with the word "vistareṇa" (in detail).
The verse is clear in its meaning.
"O Janārdana," as before;
for me, who hears your speech—which is like nectar—tasting it with both ears and tongue, there is no satiety.
Here, because the phrase "your speech" is not explicitly stated [as being identical to nectar], there is the figure of speech *apahnuti* (concealment).
Either the first type of hyperbole (atiśayokti) or the commingling (saṅkara) of those two is the poetic figure (alaṅkāra). //18//
The Blessed Lord said: Well then, I shall declare to you my divine self-manifestations.
I have described them according to their importance, O best of the Kurus; there is no end to my detailed enumeration.

Śrīdhara: Being thus entreated, the Blessed One said, "Hanta. "Hanta" is an expression of compassionate address. I shall describe to you, preeminently, those divine manifestations of My power, because there is no end to the detailed expansion of My intermediate manifestations.
Therefore, I shall describe a few of those that are the most prominent. //19//
Madhusūdana:
Here is the reply;
"Hanta" expresses assent.
"I shall do what you have requested; do not be anxious"—having thus comforted Arjuna, He begins to perform that very task:
"O best of the Kurus, I shall describe those divine glories of Myself which are well-known and unique to Me, according to their importance;
however, a description in full detail is impossible."
Since there is no end to my manifold manifestations in detail, the meaning is that I shall describe only some of those manifestations which are the most preeminent. //19//
Viśvanātha:
The word "hanta" is used here in the sense of compassion. This is because, primarily and preeminently, there is no end to the expansion of those [powers].
These manifestations (*vibhūtayaḥ*) are divine and supreme indeed, not merely things such as grass or bricks.

Here, by the word "vibhūti" (manifestation), only material and non-material entities are meant; all of these, because they have arisen from the power of the Blessed One, are intended and should be known as objects of meditation in the very form of the Blessed One, according to their respective degrees of excellence. //19//
Baladeva: Being thus questioned, the Blessed Lord said, "Hanta. The word "hanta" expresses compassion. [The worlds] are divine, meaning excellent.
But it is not grass, bricks, and so forth;
"manifestations" (*vibhūtayaḥ*) is as explained previously.
"Primarily" means by way of predominance, because there is no end to their detailed enumeration.

Here, by the word *vibhūti*, the sovereign powers (*aiśvaryas*) characterized by the nature of being the controller are to be understood, according to the *Amara-koṣa*: "Vibhūti, bhūti, and aiśvarya [are synonyms].
Both material and non-material entities are to be described as *bhūti*.
All of these are to be manifested through the power of the Lord of All and experienced within the Self of the Lord of All in a graduated manner.

Those doctrines which are stated to be the very forms of the Lord in reality are intended solely for the purpose of meditative cultivation (bhāvanā) in that form; it should be understood from the context that they are not, like other things, merely partial manifestations of His power. //19//
I am the Self, O Guḍākeśa, dwelling in the heart of all beings; I am the beginning, the middle, and indeed the end of all beings. 10.20

Śrīdhara: Therein, first He describes the divine form: "O Guḍākeśa, I am the Supreme Self (Paramātman) abiding as the controller within the hearts—the internal organs—of all beings by means of attributes such as omniscience;
'Ādi' means birth."
The middle is maintenance; the end is dissolution. The meaning is that I alone am the cause of the birth and so forth of all beings. //20//
Madhusūdana:
First of all, listen to that which is primarily to be contemplated: "I am.

You should meditate upon the Self—the mass of consciousness and bliss—which resides in the heart-region, the abode of all beings, in the form of the inner controller (antaryāmin) and as the inner self (pratyag-ātman), thinking: "I am indeed Vāsudeva."
The term "O Guḍākeśa" (he of sleep-conquered hair) indicates the capacity for meditative absorption (*dhyāna*). However,
if there is an incapacity for such meditation, then the meditations to be described hereafter must be performed.

Regarding that, he first states the object of meditation: "I alone am the beginning, the origin, and the middle—the maintenance—and the end—the destruction—of beings, that is, of living entities who are designated as conscious in the world.
The meaning is that I alone am to be meditated upon in the form of the origin, maintenance, and destruction of all classes of conscious beings, as well as in the form of their cause. //20//
Viśvanātha:
Here, first of all, he says "I am" (aham), meaning: "Meditate upon me alone as the single part that is the cause of all manifestations.
Ātman is the Supreme Self (paramātman), the Puruṣa who is the creator of the Mahat and the inner controller (antaryāmī) of Prakṛti.

The term *guḍākeśa*, meaning "one who has conquered sleep," indicates his capacity for meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). The phrase "he who dwells in the heart-essence (*āśaya*) of the Virāj who consists of all beings" refers to him as the inner controller (*antaryāmī*) of the collective Virāj (*samaṣṭi-virāḍ*).
Likewise, the phrase "dwelling in the heart-essence of all individual beings" refers to him as the inner controller of the individual Virāj (*vyaṣṭi-virāḍ*).
The beginning of beings is birth, the middle is their maintenance, and the end is their withdrawal; the meaning is that I am the cause of each of these. //20//

Baladeva: In this regard, with the intention that you should contemplate me alone—the cause of all manifestations—as the three forms beginning with the Great Creator (Mahat-sraṣṭṛ) through my own partial expansion (svāṃśa), He says, "I am the Self" (aham ātmā).
O Guḍākeśa—by this address to one who has conquered sleep, his fitness for such contemplation is revealed.

The Self, the Supreme Self consisting of the three forms beginning with the Great Creator, whose nature is the realization of manifestations and bliss, who is the referent of the word "I" (asmac-chabdārtha), and who dwells within the hearts of all beings, is to be contemplated by you.

I alone abide as the inner controller (antaryāmī) of primordial nature (prakṛti), residing within the womb of that root-nature (mūla-prakṛti)—which consists of all beings from the principle of Pradhāna down to earth—in the form of the Garbhodaka ocean. Likewise, I alone abide as the inner controller of the collective Virāṭ, residing within the womb of the Vairāja—the presiding deity of all individual souls (jīvas)—in the form of the Garbhodaka ocean.

"I alone exist within the heart of all beings and living creatures in the form of one who reclines upon the ocean of milk as the individual soul (vyaṣṭi), the cosmic soul (virāj), and the inner controller (antaryāmī). Thus, you should contemplate those three forms as my own manifestations.
In the Subālopaniṣad, Nārāyaṇa is described as the inner controller of all beings, from primordial nature (prakṛti) onwards, and as the supreme remainder (sarva-śeṣī).
In the Sātvata-tantra, three incarnations of the Supreme Person (puruṣa) are recorded: [the Vāsudeva, Saṅkarṣaṇa, and Pradyumna].
"Furthermore, they know that Viṣṇu has three forms designated as Puruṣa:
the first is the creator of the Mahat; the second is situated within the threads [of the world];
and the third resides in all beings. By knowing these, one is liberated. Thus it is said.
And these are the incarnations of Vāsudeva Kṛṣṇa—
He who, in the waters of the causal ocean, enjoyed the sleep of yoga— and so forth, according to the three verses of the Brahma-saṃhitā. (5.47)

The origin of beings is their birth, the middle is their preservation, and the end is their dissolution; I alone am the cause of each of these, characterized as the Puruṣa described by you, and thus should you contemplate me. //20//
Among the Ādityas I am Viṣṇu; among luminous bodies I am the radiant Sun; among the Maruts I am Marīci; and among the stars I am the Moon. (10.21)
Śrīdhara: Now, from the verse beginning with "Of the Ādityas" until the end of the chapter, He describes His manifestations (vibhūtis).
Among the twelve Ādityas, I am the Āditya named Viṣṇu.
Among luminaries, those that illuminate, I am the sun, Ravi, who is the radiant one endowed with rays pervading the universe.
Among the Maruts, who are a specific class of deities, I am the one named Marīci;
or else, [I am] among the seven groups of Maruts, who are the winds.
And they are the seven hosts of Maruts: Avaha, Pravaha, Vivaha, Parāvaha, Udvaha, Saṃvaha, and Parivaha.
Among the constellations, I am the Moon. //21//
Madhusūdana says that for one who is unable to do this, external meditations should be performed until the end of the chapter:
"Among the twelve Ādityas, I am Viṣṇu"— that is, the Āditya named Viṣṇu, or the Vāmana incarnation.
Among the luminaries that illuminate, I am the radiant Sun, the all-pervading illuminator;
among the Maruts, the seven groups of seven, I am he named Marīci; and among the constellations, I am the Moon, the lord of the stars—the genitive case here is used for specification.
In this context, the genitive case is generally used in the sense of specification (*nirdhāraṇa*);
occasionally it is also used in the sense of relation (*sambandha*), as in "among beings I am consciousness" (*bhūtānām asmi cetanā*) and so forth.
