Furthermore, Vāmana, Rāma, and others, though endowed with all sovereign powers (*sarvaiśvarya*), are listed among the manifestations (*vibhūtayaḥ*) in this form because they are intended to be meditated upon as such.
"I am Vāsudeva among the Vṛṣṇis"—this is stated in that form with the intention of meditation, just as [He] is recited even among His own divine manifestations.
Beyond this, since this chapter is for the most part clear in meaning, we shall provide an explanation only here and there. //21//
Viśvanātha:

Now, until the end of the chapter, he describes His manifestations (vibhūtayaḥ) using both the genitive of specification (nirdhāraṇa-ṣaṣṭhī) and, in some cases, the genitive of relation (sambandha-ṣaṣṭhī).
Among the twelve Ādityas, "I am Viṣṇu"—the meaning is that the sun bearing that name is My manifestation.
Thus, among all luminaries that illuminate everywhere, I am the sun, radiant with a great garland of rays; and I am Marīci, a particular kind of wind. //21//
Baladeva said: Among the twelve Ādityas, I am Viṣṇu as Vāmana;
among the luminaries, I am the radiant Sun whose rays pervade the universe;
and among the forty-nine Maruts, I am Marīci.
"I am the moon, the lord of the stars, the moon that showers nectar.

Here, it should be understood that the genitive case is used for specification (*nirdhāraṇa*), though it is generally employed in some instances to express a general relationship (*sambandha*). //21//
Among the Vedas, I am the Sāmaveda; among the gods, I am Vāsava; among the senses, I am the mind; and among beings, I am consciousness. 10.22
Śrīdhara: "Of the Vedas... Vāsava is Indra. Among beings, I am consciousness—the power of knowledge. //22//
Madhusūdana:
Among the four Vedas, I am the Sāmaveda, most delightful by virtue of its melodic sweetness;
and among the Vasus, I am Indra, the sovereign of all the gods.
The mind is the activator of the eleven sense organs.
Among the transformations of the elements related to all living beings, I am the consciousness—the function of the intellect that manifests pure awareness. //22//
Viśvanātha: Vāsava is Indra. The consciousness belonging to beings is the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti). //22//
Baladeva: Among the Vedas, I am the Sāmaveda, because of its excellence in the sweetness of its song;
among the gods, I am Vāsava, their king Indra;
and among the senses, I am the mind, which is difficult to conquer and the impeller of them all.
I am the consciousness, the power of knowledge, belonging to all beings. //22//
Among the Rudras I am Śaṅkara; among the Yakṣas and Rākṣasas I am the Lord of Wealth; among the Vasus I am Pāvaka; and among the peaked mountains I am Meru. 10.23.
Śrīdhara: Regarding the phrase "of the Rudras," the Rākṣasas are also mentioned together with the Yakṣas because of their similarity in traits such as cruelty;
among them, I am Kuvera, the lord of wealth.
Pāvaka is fire;
among those possessing peaks—that is, among those that are lofty—Meru is the foremost. //23//
Madhusūdana:
Among the eleven Rudras, Śaṅkara is one;
Vitteśa is the lord of wealth, Kubera, who is [the ruler] of the Yakṣas and Rākṣasas.
Among the eight Vasus, I am Pāvaka; among the peaked mountains, the most lofty summits, I am Meru, the Sumeru. //23//
Viśvanātha is the Lord of Wealth, Kuvera. //23//
Baladeva said: Among the eleven Rudras, I am the Rudra named Śaṅkara;
among the Yakṣas and Rākṣasas, I am their sovereign, Kuvera the lord of wealth;
and among the eight Vasus, I am Pāvaka, the fire.
Among the exceedingly lofty peaks, I am Meru, the golden mountain. //23//
O Pārtha, know me to be Bṛhaspati, the chief among the domestic priests;
among army commanders I am Skanda, and among bodies of water I am the ocean. 10.24
Śrīdhara says: "Among the domestic priests"—know me to be Bṛhaspati, the foremost among domestic priests because he is the priest of the gods;
"among the generals"—I am Skanda, the commander-in-chief of the divine armies.
Among all bodies of water, whether flowing streams or still reservoirs, I am the ocean.
Madhusūdana says:

O Pārtha, know—that is, understand—that Me alone is Bṛhaspati, the priest of Indra; for since Indra is the best among all kings, Bṛhaspati is the foremost and most excellent among all priests and royal chaplains.
Among generals and army commanders, I am Skanda Guha, the commander of the celestial host;
among bodies of water, that is, among divine reservoirs such as lakes and ponds, I am the ocean, the reservoir dug by the sons of Sagara. //24//
Viśvanātha:
"Of the army commanders" is an archaic (ārṣa) usage.
Skandha is Kārtikeya. //24//
Baladeva says: Since Indra is the chief of all kings, know me to be Bṛhaspati, his priest, the lord of all and the foremost among royal priests; such is the meaning of "I am he.
As for the form *senānīnām*, the insertion of the augment *nuṭ* is an archaic (Vedic) usage.
Among the armies of all kings, I am Skanda Kārttikeya.
Among all bodies of water with stagnant waters, I am the ocean. //24//
Among the great seers, I am Bhṛgu; among words, I am the single syllable Om;
among sacrifices, I am the sacrifice of silent recitation (japa-yajña); and among immovable things, I am the Himalaya. 10.25
Śrīdhara: Regarding the phrase "of the great sages":
among the words—that is, among the utterances consisting of syllables—I am the single syllable known as Oṃ.
Among sacrifices—both those prescribed by the Vedas (śrauta) and those based on tradition (smārta)—I am the sacrifice in the form of silent recitation (japa). //25//
Madhusūdana says:

Among the seven great sages (maharṣis) who are the [seven] Brahmās, I am Bhṛgu because of my supreme splendor. Among words—that is, among speech characterized by syllables—I am the single syllable, the word *oṃkāra*.
Among sacrifices, I am indeed the sacrifice of silent recitation (*japa-yajña*), for it is the most purifying because it is free from defects such as violence.

Among stationary things (*sthāvara*) that possess stability, I am the Himalaya; among peaked mountains, I am Meru. Since it has been stated thus, there is no fault in the difference of meaning based on being "stationary" and being "peaked. //25//
Viśvanātha:
The single syllable is the Praṇava. //25//
Baladeva: Among the great sages, the sons of Brahmā, I am Bhṛgu, the most radiant.
Among words characterized by their syllables, among all utterances, I am the single syllable, the *praṇava*.
Among sacrifices, I am the sacrifice of silent recitation (*japa-yajña*).
Because it is superior by virtue of its non-violent nature, I am the Himācala among the stationary, stable things;
yet, due to the difference in meaning between "extreme height" and "extreme stability," there is a distinction between the splendors of Meru and the Himalaya. //25//
Among all trees, the Aśvattha; among the divine seers, Nārada;
among the Gandharvas, Citraratha; and among the Siddhas, the sage Kapila. //26//
Śrīdhara: Regarding "Aśvattha":
among those who, being gods themselves, attained the status of seers (*ṛṣi*) through the vision of mantras, I am Nārada;
among the perfected ones (*siddha*), who have realized the ultimate reality from their very birth, I am the sage named Kapila. //26//
Madhusūdana says:
Among all these trees, forest giants, and others,
I am Nārada among the divine sages (devarṣis)— those who, being gods themselves, attained the status of sages through their vision of the mantras.
Among the Gandharvas, who by their very nature sing to the gods, I am Citraratha;

among the Siddhas, who from birth have attained a preeminent excellence in virtue, knowledge, dispassion, and sovereignty without effort, and who have realized the supreme truth, I am the sage Kapila. 26.
Viśvanātha: Nothing.
Baladeva: Among all trees, I am the Aśvattha tree because of its venerability; among the divine sages (devarṣis), I am Nārada because of my excellence as a supreme devotee;
and among the Gandharvas, I am Citraratha because of my excellence as a preeminent singer.
Among the Siddhas who possess the innate powers such as atomization (aṇimā) and the rest, I am the sage Kapila Kārdami. //26//
Among horses, know me to be Uccaiḥśravas, born of the nectar;
among lordly elephants, Airāvata; and among men, the sovereign of men. 27.

Śrīdhara: Regarding the phrase "Uccaiḥśravas," know that the horse named Uccaiḥśravas, who emerged from the churning of the Ocean of Milk for the sake of the nectar of immortality (*amṛta*), is My manifestation (*vibhūti*).
The expression "born of the nectar" (*amṛtodbhava*) is also to be connected with Airāvata.
Know me as the king, the lord of men, who is my own manifestation. //27//
Madhusūdana said:
"Know me to be Uccaiḥśravas, the horse born from the churning for nectar, in the midst of horses;
know me to be Airāvata, the lordly elephant born from the churning for nectar, in the midst of elephants."
And among men, know me to be the king, the lord of men; this is to be supplied [to the verse]. //27//
Viśvanātha:
"Amṛtodbhavam" means that which arose from the churning for nectar. //27//

Baladeva said: "Know me to be Uccaiḥśravas among horses and Airāvata among the lordly elephants. 'Born from the nectar' (amṛtodbhava) is an epithet for both, meaning born from the churning of the ocean of milk for the sake of the nectar."
The king, a lord of men, possessed irresistible splendor and was most righteous. //27//
Among weapons, I am the thunderbolt; among cows, I am the wish-fulfilling cow; I am Kandarpa, the progenitor; and among serpents, I am Vāsuki. 28.
Śrīdhara: Regarding the phrase "of weapons," among weapons I am the thunderbolt (*vajra*). [The term] *kāmadhuk* means that which milks out desires.
I am Kandarpa, the god of love, who is the cause of procreation and the origin of offspring.
My manifestation is not merely desire characterized by sensual enjoyment alone, for such desire is contrary to the scriptures.
Among serpents, I am Vāsuki, the king of the snakes. (28)
Madhusūdana says:
Among weapons and missiles, I am the thunderbolt, that weapon produced from the bones of Dadhīci;
among milch cows, I am the "wish-milker" (kāmadhuk), so called because it milks out every desire.
I am Vasiṣṭha’s wish-granting cow (kāmadhenu), born from the churning of the ocean.
Among desires, I am procreation—the desire for the generation of offspring, which is the god of love (kandarpa).
The word "ca" (and) is used here to exclude the kind of desire that is merely a cause for sensual pleasure.
Serpents and nāgas are distinguished by their different species;
among those serpents, I am Vāsuki, their king. (28)
Viśvanātha:
I am the wish-fulfilling cow, the granter of desires; among the gods of love, I am Kandarpa, the progenitor, the cause of the birth of offspring. //28//
Baladeva: Among weapons, I am the thunderbolt, the Pavī;
I am the wish-fulfilling cow, the fulfiller of desires;
I am Kandarpa, the god of love, the progenitor who produces offspring.
And because of the word "and" (*ca*), it is implied: "He is merely the cause of the pleasure of sexual passion, but I am not.
Among the single-headed serpents, I am Vāsuki. (28)
Among the serpents I am Ananta; among the aquatic creatures I am Varuṇa; among the ancestors I am Aryaman; and among those who exercise restraint, I am Yama. 10.29
Śrīdhara: "Ananta" means that among the non-venomous serpents (nāgas), I am Ananta Śeṣa, their king;
among aquatic creatures (yādas), I am Varuṇa, their king.
Among the ancestors, I am Aryaman;
among those who exercise restraint, I am Yama, the one who ordains discipline. //29//
Madhusūdana:
Among the various species of serpents, I am Ananta, known as Śeṣa, who is their king;
among aquatic creatures, I am Varuṇa, who is their king.
Among the Pitṛs, I am the king of the Pitṛs named Aryaman;
among those who exercise restraint—bestowing favor through the granting of the fruits of dharma and adharma and exercising punishment—I am Yama. (29)
Viśvanātha: [He is] the restrainer—meaning the punisher—of the *yādas*, that is, those who move in the water. //29//
Baladeva: Among the many-headed serpents, I am Ananta Śeṣa;
among the aquatic creatures, I am Varuṇa, their lord;
among the ancestors, I am the king known as Aryaman, the deity of the manes.
Among those who restrain and those who punish, I am Yama, the one who inflicts justice; the absence of the suffix *cha* is an archaic Vedic usage. //29//
Among the Daityas I am Prahlāda; among those who reckon, I am Time; among beasts I am the king of beasts, and among birds I am Vainateya. (10.30)
Śrīdhara says:
"Among those who reckon—that is, those who subdue or calculate—I am Time (Kāla).
The king of beasts is the lion."
Among birds, I am Vainateya Garuḍa. //30//
Madhusūdana:

Among the Daityas, those of the lineage of Diti, I am Prahlāda, for I delight and gladden all through my supreme goodness (sattva). And among those who reckon—that is, those performing calculation—I am Time (Kāla).
Among animals and beasts, I am the lion, the king of beasts; and among birds, I am Vainateya, Garuḍa, the son of Vinatā. //30//
Viśvanātha: the Lord of the Universe;
mṛgendraḥ: the king of beasts, the lion; kalayatām: of those who subjugate or bring under control.
Vainateya is Garuḍa. //30//

Baladeva: Among the Daityas, those of the lineage of Diti, I am Prahlāda, the most excellent because of my supreme devotion to the Blessed One. Among those who subdue or bring others under their control, I am Time (Kāla).
Among wild beasts, I am the king of beasts, the lion, preeminent due to his extraordinary prowess.
Among birds, I am Vainateya Garuḍa, who is preeminent as the vehicle of Viṣṇu. //30//
Among purifiers I am the wind; among weapon-bearers I am Rāma; among fish I am the Makara; and among flowing streams I am the Ganges. (10.31)
Śrīdhara: Regarding "pavana":
among those that purify (*pāvayitṛ*), or among those that possess speed (*vegavat*), I am Vāyu. Among weapon-wielders, that is, among heroes, I am Rāma, the son of Daśaratha.
Or rather, Rāma is Paraśurāma;
among the *jhaṣas*, that is, among fish, I am the species of fish called the Makara; and among the currents, that is, among flowing waters, I am the Bhāgīrathī. //31//
Among those that purify, or among those that are swift, I am the wind, Pavana.
Among the wielders of weapons— those skilled in battle— I am Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, the supreme hero who brought about the destruction of the entire race of Rākṣasas.

It was stated previously that this reading is included here for the purpose of meditating upon the Lord’s essential nature even in this form, just as in the statement, "Among the Vṛṣṇis, I am Vāsudeva.

Among the *jhaṣas*, which are fish, I am the one called the *makara*, a specific species thereof. Among the currents—rivers with water flowing with force—I am the Ganges, the Jāhnavī, the best of all rivers. //31//
Viśvanātha:

Among those who purify (pavitrīkurvatām), or among those who are swift (vegavatām), Rāma—namely Paraśurāma—is [included] because he is an incarnation through possession (āveśāvatāra); and since possessions (āveśas) are specific types of individual souls (jīva-viśeṣa), it is entirely appropriate that he possesses the status of a manifestation (vibhūti).
Accordingly, there is a statement from the Padma Purāṇa cited in the Bhāgavatāmṛta:
This has been told to you, O Goddess, the life-story of the high-souled Jāmadagnya,
the Lord who wields the Śārṅga bow, concerning his incarnation through the penetration of Śakti;
and it is said that he became possessed by the Bhārgava.
And the definition of the descent through possession (*āveśāvatāra*) is found in that same *Bhāgavatāmṛta*:

"Those living beings who are possessed by Janārdana through a portion of His powers such as knowledge and so forth are called 'possessions' (*āveśa*); they are indeed the greatest of souls. (LBhāg 1.1.18)
Among the *jhaṣas*, that is, fish, the *makara* is a specific species of fish;
[he is the lord] of the *srotas*, that is, of the flowing rivers. //31//
Baladeva says: Among those that purify, among the purifiers, and among the swift, I am Pavana, the wind;
Rāma refers to Paraśurāma;
and among the fish, I am the Makara, a specific species thereof.
Among the streams with their flowing waters, I am the Jāhnavī, the Gaṅgā. //31//
O Arjuna, I am the beginning, the end, and also the middle of all creations; among sciences, I am the science of the Self (adhyātma-vidyā); and among those who debate, I am the discourse. 10.32.
Śrīdhara: Regarding the phrase "of creations" (*sargāṇām*):
they are called "creations" (*sarga*) because they are created; these are space and the other elements.
Of these, I am both their beginning and their end, as well as their middle.

In the passage "I am the beginning and the middle," the supreme sovereignty consisting of being the agent of creation and so forth was stated; here, however, the distinction is that origination, maintenance, and dissolution are declared to be meditated upon as My manifestations (vibhūti). Adhyātma-vidyā is the knowledge of the Self.

Among the three types of discourse— vāda, jalpa, and vitaṇḍā— which are well known among disputing speakers, I am the vāda. In that [discourse], both parties establish their own positions through valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa) and reasoning (tarka), and one refutes the opponent's position by means of quibbles (chala), futile rejoinders (jāti), and points of defeat (nigrahasthāna), but does not [refute] one's own position.
That which is called *vitaṇḍā* (cavil) is a type of discourse.
Among these, *jalpa* (disputation) and *vitaṇḍā* have as their sole fruit the examination of the relative strength of two disputants who desire victory.
*Vāda* (discussion), however, has the determination of truth as its fruit, occurring between two persons free from passion, such as a teacher and a student, or others.
Therefore, because of its excellence, it is my manifestation;
this is the meaning. //32//
Madhusūdana:
I alone am the beginning, the end, and the middle—the creation, sustenance, and dissolution—of all emanations, that is, of all insentient creations;
O Arjuna!
In the opening [verse], it was stated that the beginning, end, and middle belong only to those beings (*bhūta*) known to be sentient because they are possessed of a living soul (*jīva*);
however, here it refers to insentient creations (*acetana-sarga*), so there is no tautology.
Among the various sciences (*vidyā*), the science of the self (*adhyātma-vidyā*)—the knowledge of the reality of the Self (*ātma-tattva-vidyā*) which is the cause of liberation—is "I."
Among the various types of discourse—namely *vāda*, *jalpa*, and *vitaṇḍā*—belonging to those who debate, I am *vāda*.

Just as in the phrase "among beings (*bhūtānām*) I am consciousness (*cetanā*)," the word *bhūta* indicates by implication (*lakṣaṇā*) the transformations belonging to them, so here the word *pravadat* (those who debate) indicates by implication the different types of discourse belonging to them; thus, the justification for this selection (*nirdhāraṇa*) is established.
According to the literal sense, however, the genitive case is used for both relations.

In that context, *vāda* (debate) is the adoption of a proponent's position (*pakṣa*) and its counter-position (*pratipakṣa*), consisting of proof and refutation by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and reasoning (*tarka*), which aims at the determination of reality (*tattva-nirṇaya*) and is carried out by two seekers of truth who are free from passion— whether they be fellow celibates or teacher and disciple.

Thus it has been said: "Debate (*vāda*) is the adoption of a thesis and its counter-thesis, employing means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and reasoning (*tarka*), characterized by refutation and defense, not contradicting established tenets (*siddhānta*), and consisting of the five members.

For the sake of protecting the determination of truth (*tattva-nirṇaya*), which is the fruit of debate, by refuting obstinate disputants, there are the two forms of discourse—*jalpa* and *vitaṇḍā*—which belong to those desiring victory and culminate merely in winning or losing.

As it has been said: "For the sake of protecting the determination of truth, *jalpa* and *vitaṇḍā* exist, like the covering of branches with thorns for the sake of protecting the growth of seeds" [Nyāyasūtra 4.2.47].

The refutation of the opponent's position by means of quibbles (chala), futile rejoinders (jāti), and points of defeat (nigrahasthāna) is common to both debate (jalpa) and destructive criticism (vitaṇḍā).
However, in that case, in destructive criticism, one party indeed establishes their own position, while the other merely refutes it.
In *jalpa*, however, the distinction is that both parties establish their own positions and both parties refute the opposing positions.

As it has been said: "Jalpa is the employment of means of proof and the detection of flaws, employing the previously mentioned [fallacies], quibbles (*chala*), futile rejoinders (*jāti*), and points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*); that same [discourse] is *vitaṇḍā* when it is devoid of the establishment of a counter-position."
Therefore, because it consists of two types of *vitaṇḍā*, that which is called *jalpa* is not a single form of debate;
rather, the authors of the *Khaṇḍana* maintain that it proceeds merely by means of a formal agreement (*samaya-bandha*) for the purpose of knowing the excellence of one's own power.
However, it has already been stated that *vāda* is superior because it culminates in the ascertainment of reality (*tattva-adhyavasāya*). //32//
Viśvanātha:
"Creations" (sargas) are those things being created, such as ether and the rest; their beginning is creation, their end is dissolution, and their middle is preservation.
The meaning is that creation, maintenance, and dissolution are to be meditated upon as My manifestations (vibhūti).
In the phrase "I am the beginning and the middle," it is the Supreme Lord alone who is declared to be the creator of the world and so forth.
Among all branches of knowledge (*vidyā*), that is, among all forms of wisdom (*jñāna*), I am the science of the Self (*ātma-vidyā*), which is the knowledge of the Self.

Among those who debate—meaning those who engage in discourse (*jalpa*), cavil (*vitaṇḍā*), and the like, consisting of the establishment of one's own position and the refutation of the opposing position—I am the discussion (*vāda*) which results in the determination of truth according to the established tenets (*siddhānta*). (32)

Baladeva: The meaning is that I am the beginning, the end, and the middle of the creations—the insentient emanations such as the *mahat* and so forth; thus, their creation, destruction, and maintenance are to be understood as My manifestations (*vibhūti*).

In the verse beginning with "I am the beginning," it was stated that My manifestation is the cause of the creation and so forth of those beings who are sentient and are portions of My own self; therefore, there is no tautology.
The limbs [of the Veda] are the four Vedas, Mīmāṃsā, and the extensive system of Nyāya.
The Dharmaśāstra and the Purāṇa—these indeed are the fourteen branches of knowledge.

Among the sciences (vidyās) thus mentioned, the science of the inner self (adhyātma-vidyā)—the Vedānta science characterized by four marks which determines the Supreme Self along with its adjuncts—is "I alone"; this is the meaning. That which is the discourse (vāda) belonging to those who debate is "I.
For among them, three types of discourse are well known: vāda, jalpa, and vitaṇḍā.
Among these, *jalpa* (wrangling) is a debate between two parties seeking victory,

wherein both establish their own positions through means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and reasoning (*tarka*), and refute the opponent's position by means of quibbles (*chala*), futile rejoinders (*jāti*), and points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*). *Vitaṇḍā* (cavil) is a debate that consists in the refutation of the opponent's position without establishing one's own, ending with the mere discrediting of the other side.
When two persons desiring victory debate for the mere purpose of testing each other's power, it is fruitless; however, a discussion between those seeking to know the truth is called *vāda*.
Because it has the determination of truth as its fruit and is thus superior, it is my manifestation (*vibhūti*). //32//
Among letters, I am the letter *a*; among compounds, I am the dual.
I alone am inexhaustible time; I am the Ordainer whose face is turned everywhere. (10.33)
Śrīdhara: "Among the syllables" means: among the syllables, that is, the letters, I am the letter *a*. This is because it is the most excellent, as it constitutes the entirety of speech.

And thus says the Śruti: "The letter *a* is indeed all speech; this very [speech], when manifested by the consonants (*sparśa*) and semivowels (*ūṣman*), becomes manifold and takes on various forms" (Ai. Ā. 1.3.6).

Among the collection of compounds—that is, among the group of compound words—I am the *dvandva* compound, such as "Rāma and Kṛṣṇa," because of its excellence due to the predominance of both members of the compound.
I alone am time in the form of an inexhaustible flow;
as for the statement "I am Time among those who calculate," therein time is described as consisting of the calculation of lifespan, having the nature of a life-span of a hundred years and so forth.
And that [time] is exhausted when that lifespan has been spent.
But here, the distinction is that time is said to be of the nature of a continuous flow and inexhaustible.
Among those who ordain the fruits of action, I am the Ordainer whose face is turned everywhere;
the meaning is: "I am the ordainer of the fruits of all actions. //33//
Madhusūdana:
Among all letters and phonemes, I am the letter *a*.
Its preeminence is well known from the Vedic revelation: "The letter *a* is indeed all speech" (Ai. Ā. 1.3.6).

Among the collection of compounds (*sāmāsika*), I am the *dvandva* compound, which has both members as its primary referents. The *avyayībhāva* has the first member as its primary referent; the *tatpuruṣa* has the second member as its primary referent; and the *bahuvrīhi* has a referent other than the members as its primary referent. Because these latter types lack the equality of both members as primary referents, they are inferior.
Therefore, I alone am that which is celebrated in such Vedic texts as "I am imperishable Time, the Knower, the Time of time, the possessor of qualities, and the knower of all sciences."
However, in the statement "I am Time among those who calculate," Time is said to be subject to decay; this is the distinction.
Among those who ordain the fruits of actions, "I am the Ordainer facing all directions"—that is, the Lord who bestows the fruits of all actions from every side—such is the meaning. //33//
Viśvanātha:
Among all compound words (*sāmāsika*), the *dvandva* is the most excellent because it gives primary importance to the meaning of both constituent parts.
Among those who destroy, I am Akṣaya Kāla, Rudra Mahākāla; and among those who create, I am Viśvatomukha, the four-faced Brahmā, the Ordainer. //33//
Baladeva: Among the letters, that is, among the phonemes, I am the letter *a*.
For the Śruti declares: "The letter *a* is indeed all speech" (Ai. Ā.
1.3.6). And among the compounds, that is, among the collection of compound words, I am the *dvandva* (copulative) compound.

Among the *avyayībhāva*, *tatpuruṣa*, and *bahuvrīhi* compounds—which lack the predominance of the meanings of both constituent words—he is superior because he possesses the predominance of the meanings of both words;
among all things that withdraw [the world], he is the imperishable one.
I am Kālāgni, the Time-fire arising from the mouth of Saṅkarṣaṇa.
Among the creators, I am the four-faced Dhātṛ, Vidhi, whose face is turned in every direction. //33//
I am death that carries off all, and I am the origin of those who are yet to be; among women, I am fame, fortune, speech, memory, intelligence, fortitude, and forgiveness.

Śrīdhara: "Among those who bring about destruction, I am Mṛtyu, the all-destroyer. Among those destined for the future—those living beings whose welfare is yet to come—I am Udbhava, their manifestation."
Among women, I am those such as Kīrti (Fame) and others who possess the forms of the six deities;
by the mere association with their reflection, living beings become praiseworthy—those women, such as Kīrti and the rest, are my manifestations. //34//
Madhusūdana:
Among those who cause destruction, I am Mṛtyu, the all-destroyer, the one who effects the dissolution of all.
And among those destined for the future—those whose welfare is yet to come—I am that very source, their excellence and rise.
Among women, I alone am the seven wives of Dharma: Fame (Kīrti), Prosperity (Śrī), Speech (Vāk), Memory (Smṛti), Intelligence (Medhā), Fortitude (Dhṛti), and Forbearance (Kṣamā).
Among these, Fame is that renown based on righteousness, consisting in being known by people from various regions and directions as being praiseworthy.
Prosperity is the perfection of virtue, wealth, and pleasure, or it is bodily splendor or radiance.
Speech is Sarasvatī, the refined voice that illuminates every meaning;
by the word "and" (ca), her consorts Mūrti and the others are also included.
Memory is the power of recollecting objects experienced long ago.
*Medhā* is the capacity for retaining the meaning of numerous texts.
*Dhṛti* is the power to sustain the aggregate of the body and the sense-faculties even in the face of despondency;
or, it is the power to turn back restlessness (*cāpalya*) when it has arisen due to the cause of unrestrained activity.
Forgiveness is the state of an unchanging mind amidst joy and sorrow.
It is well known that among all women, those whose very connection—even by mere appearance—makes a person worthy of the respect of the entire world, possess the highest excellence. //34//
Viśvanātha:
Among the momentary deaths, I am the death that takes away everything and robs one of all memory—of which it is said, "death is ultimate forgetfulness.
Among the future modifications of living beings, I am the first modification, arising.

Among women, I am fame (kīrti), renown (khyāti), fortune (śrī), splendor (kānti), and speech (vāk)—the latter being remembered as Vāṇī; likewise, I am the four beginning with Smṛti, and by the word "and" (ca), others such as Mūrti and other wives of Dharma. //34//
Baladeva: Among deaths that occur at every moment, I am the death that takes away all memory.
Among the future transformations of living beings, I am the first transformation called birth.
Among women, the seven beginning with Kīrti are My divine manifestations.
For these are indeed goddesses,
by whose mere radiance men become praiseworthy;
therein, "fame" (kīrti) is the renown for one's virtuous qualities, such as righteousness and so forth.
The glorious attainment of the three aims of life, or the radiance of the body; speech that manifests all meanings, namely the Sanskrit language;
and memory, which is the power of recollecting experienced objects.
*Medhā* is the capacity for discerning the meaning of many scriptures;
*dhṛti* is the capacity to turn back from restlessness when it has arisen;
and *kṣamā* is the state of a mind free from perturbation when joy or sorrow is encountered. //34//
Among the Sāmans, I am the Bṛhat-sāman; likewise, among meters, I am the Gāyatrī.
Among months, I am Mārgaśīrṣa; among seasons, I am the flower-bearing spring. //35//

Śrīdhara: "Bṛhatsāman" refers to the Bṛhatsāman sung upon this verse, *tvām iddhi havāmahe* (Rg Veda 6.46.1). By means of that, Indra is praised for his status as the Lord of All; thus, there is preeminence (*śraiṣṭhya*).

Among the mantras distinguished by their power of will (*chanda*), I am the *gāyatrī* mantra, because it is the most excellent for bestowing the status of the twice-born and for the fetching of the Soma. I am Kusumākara, the spring season. (35)
Madhusūdana:

It was stated that among the Vedas, "I am the Sāmaveda"; regarding that, there is this further distinction: among the specific melodies (*gīti-viśeṣa*) based on the syllables of the *ṛks*, the specific melody upon the verse beginning with "tvām iddhi havāmahe" (Rgveda 6.46.1) is the Bṛhat-sāman.

And that *pṛṣṭha-stotra* at the *atirātra* sacrifice—which consists of a hymn of praise to Indra as the Lord of All—is "I" (*aham*), because it is superior to others. Among the *ṛcs*, which are distinguished by their meter (*chandas*) characterized by fixed syllables and feet, it is the "twice-born" (*dvijāti*) because it is the cause of the second birth;

it "pervades" the three pressings, beginning with the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*); and it is [superior] to the *triṣṭubh* and *jagatī* meters, which went forth for the purpose of fetching the Soma.

Soma was not obtained and four syllables were lost: three from the Jagatī and one from the Triṣṭubh. Because of those syllables and because of the bringing back of Soma, I, the Gāyatrī verse, am the most excellent of all. Indeed, in the beginning, the meters had four syllables each; then the Jagatī flew toward Soma, and having left behind three syllables, she departed. Thereafter...
The *triṣṭubh* flew toward Soma; she flew away, leaving behind one syllable. Then the *gāyatrī* flew toward Soma;

she returned, bringing back those syllables as well as Soma. Therefore, beginning with "the *gāyatrī* has eight syllables," the *Śatapatha-śruti* states: "All pressings (*savana*) are indeed *gāyatra*, for the *gāyatrī* is that which is being brought near."
And from the Chāndogya Upaniṣad scripture: "The Gāyatrī indeed is all this that has come to be," and so forth.

Among the twelve months, I am Mārgaśīrṣa, which—abounding in vāstūka greens, leafy vegetables, and the like—is a cause of happiness due to its lack of cold and heat. Among the six seasons, I am Vasanta, the maker of flowers, the most delightful source of all fragrant blossoms.
One should initiate a Brāhmaṇa in the spring;
a Brāhmaṇa should establish the sacred fires in the spring;
one should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma every spring.
One should indeed begin this during the spring;
for spring is the season of the Brahmin—thus I am well-known through such scriptural authorities. //35//
Viśvanātha:
It has been stated, "Among the Vedas, I am the Sāmaveda.
Within that, among the Sāmans as well, the Bṛhatsāman is the one sung in this Ṛgvedic verse: "We indeed invoke you with the Bṛhat-sāman" (ṚV 6.46.1).
Among meters, the meter named Gāyatrī is [the first];
the flower-maker is spring. //35//
Baladeva: It was stated previously that "among the Vedas, I am the Sāmaveda.
Regarding that, he mentions another distinction with the word "Bṛhat":
among the specific chants (*gīti*) of the Sāmans which are based on the syllables of the *ṛks*, [it is] "We truly invoke you" (*iddhi havāmahe*, Rv 6.46.1).

In this verse, I am the specific melody (*gīti*), the Bṛhat-sāman; and that, in the Atirātra sacrifice, is the Pṛṣṭha-stotra, consisting of praise to Indra as the Lord of All, because it is superior to other Sāmans. Among the *ṛks*—which are verses distinguished by their meter (*chandas*) consisting of fixed syllables and feet—I am the Gāyatrī verse, because of its preeminence as the cause of the second birth for the twice-born.
Furthermore, because it is heard [in scripture] that "Gāyatrī indeed is this entire world, whatever exists here," she possesses the status of an incarnation of Brahman;
and because, through the excellence of her new harvests and other qualities, Mārgaśīrṣa is superior to other months;
and because, by being free from cold and heat, consisting of various fragrant flowers, and being the cause of my festival, Kusumākara (Vasanta) is superior to other seasons. //35//
Of those who deceive with dice, I am the game; of the radiant, I am the splendor;
I am victory; I am resolve; and of those possessed of goodness, I am the goodness. (10.36)
Śrīdhara:
Of those who play with deceit, intent on mutual cheating, I am gambling;
of the radiant, the powerful, I am their splendor and majesty.
Among victors, I am victory; among those possessed of resolve, I am resolve—the exertion of the energetic; and among those endowed with goodness, I am goodness. //36//
Madhusūdana:

Among those who employ deceit—that is, those who practice deception through fraud such as gambling with dice and the like—I am the gambling that causes the loss of all one's possessions. Among the radiant—those possessing exceedingly fierce power—I am their splendor, which consists of unimpeded authority.
Among victors, I am victory characterized by superiority over those who have been defeated.
Among the resolute, I am resolve—the effort whose fruit is never-failing.

Among the virtuous, that is, those possessed of *sattva*, I am *sattva* itself, which here refers to the effects of *sattva* characterized by righteousness, knowledge, dispassion, and sovereignty. (36)
Viśvanātha:
Among those intent on deceiving one another, I am the gambling match;
among the victors, I am victory.
Among those who possess resolve, I am their resolve;
among those who possess strength, I am their strength. //36//
Baladeva says: Of those who practice deceit, that is, those who engage in mutual deception, I am the gambling match involving the stake of one's entire possessions, such as the casting of dice;
and of the radiant, that is, those possessed of power, I am their splendor and majesty.
I am these.
Among victors, I am victory characterized by superiority over those who have been defeated;
I am the victory belonging to victors. Among the resolute, I am the resolve belonging to those who exert themselves.
I am the successful effort;
I am the courage and the strength belonging to those who possess courage and strength. //36//
Among the Vṛṣṇis I am Vāsudeva; among the Pāṇḍavas, Dhananjaya;
among the sages, too, I am Vyāsa; and among the poets, the poet Uśanas. (10.37)
Śrīdhara: "Of the Vṛṣṇis" means I, who am instructing you, am Vāsudeva;
and you yourself, O Dhanañjaya, are my manifestation (vibhūti).

Among the sages (*muni*), those whose nature is to contemplate the meaning of the Vedas, I am Veda-vyāsa; among the poets (*kavi*), those who possess far-reaching vision, I am the poet named Uśanas, also known as Śukra. //37//
Madhusūdana:

It has already been stated that Madhusūdana is mentioned even among the manifestations (vibhūtis) of the Lord himself for the purpose of meditation in that form. Among the Vṛṣṇis, I am Vāsudeva—the son of Vasudeva—who is well-known as your teacher.
Likewise, among the Pāṇḍavas, you are Dhananjaya, and I am he;
among the sages whose nature is contemplation, I am Vedavyāsa;
and among the poets who possess far-reaching vision and discern subtle meanings, I am Uśanas, the poet known as Śukra. //37//
Viśvanātha:
Among the Vṛṣṇis, Vāsudeva—that is, Vasudeva, my father—is my manifestation (*vibhūti*).

The suffix *aṇ* is used here in its own sense (*svārthika*) because the word belongs to the *prajñādi* group [according to Pāṇini 5.4.38]. Since it was not stated that "I alone am among the Vṛṣṇis," it is not intended for this [Vasudeva] to have any other purpose [than being a manifestation]. //37//
Baladeva: Among the Vṛṣṇis, I am Saṅkarṣaṇa, the son of Vasudeva, and not Vāsudeva;
for it is inappropriate to explain "Vāsudeva" as "I am Kṛṣṇa," since [Kṛṣṇa] is the Lord himself, whereas [Saṅkarṣaṇa] is His manifestation (vibhūti).

Even though Mahat-sraṣṭṛ and others, as well as Vāmana, Kapila, and so forth, are directly the Lord, their description as manifestations is justified because they are partial incarnations (svāṃśāvatāra), or because there is a desire to represent them as objects of meditation in those specific forms.
And being a part of oneself (*svāṃśatva*) should be understood as having all powers unmanifested. Among the Pāṇḍavas, I am Dhananjaya,
because of my superiority over the others due to not being [merely] an incarnation (*avatāra*).
Among the sages (*munis*) who are devoted to contemplating the meaning of the divine, I am Vyāsa Bādarāyaṇa;
for, as one of my own incarnations, he is superior to all others.
Among the poets (*kavis*) who discern subtle meanings, I am Uśanas Śukra.
He who is known as the Seer (Kavi). //37//
Among those who subdue, I am the rod of punishment; among those who seek victory, I am statesmanship; among secrets, I am silence; and among the wise, I am knowledge. (10.38)
Śrīdhara: "I am the rod. Among those who subdue—that is, among those who exercise restraint—I am the rod. That rod by which even the unrestrained become restrained is my manifestation.
For those who wish to conquer, I am the policy of conciliation (*sāman*), which is the very form of a strategic means.
Among secrets that must be guarded, I am silence—the state of not speaking—which is the cause for their protection;
for the intention of one who remains silent is not known.
That which is the knowledge of the wise—those who know reality—that I am. //38//
Madhusūdana:
For those who seek to subdue the unsubdued, I am the rod of punishment—the cause of restraint for those who have strayed from the path and must be set back upon it.
For those who desire to conquer, I am policy—the logic that reveals the means of victory.
Among the secret things—that is, those things to be guarded—I am silence, which is the cause of guarding them, namely the restraint of speech;
for the intention of one who remains silent is not known.

Among the secret things to be guarded, I am that silence characterized by the profound meditation (*nididhyāsana*) upon the Self, preceded by hearing and reflecting [on the scriptures] along with renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*).

I am that knowledge belonging to the wise—the possessors of wisdom—which arises from the maturation of hearing, reflection, and meditative absorption; which consists of the direct realization of the non-dual Self; and which is the adversary of all ignorance.
I am the rod belonging to those who subdue [the wicked]. (38)
Baladeva: I am the punishment belonging to those who punish—that is, those who wield the rod of justice;
the meaning is that punishment, by which those who have gone astray are made to walk on the path of the righteous, is My manifestation.
I am the policy belonging to those who desire victory—those who wish to conquer; that is, I am the principle of right conduct (*nīti*).

Because it is superior to the secret [teachings] through hearing and so forth, I am the knowledge pertaining to those respective objects belonging to the possessors of knowledge—those who know the reality of the higher and the lower. //38//
And whatever is the seed of all beings, that too I am, O Arjuna; there is no being, whether moving or unmoving, that can exist without me. 39.

Śrīdhara: Regarding the phrase "And that which..."—and furthermore, I am the seed of all beings, the cause of their growth. The reason for this is: there is no being whatsoever, whether moving or unmoving, that could exist without me. //39//
Madhusūdana:
Furthermore, O Arjuna, that which is the seed— the cause of the growth of all beings— is indeed I myself, the consciousness conditioned by Māyā.
Whatever exists in this world, whether moving or non-moving, that would exist without me does not exist at all; for the meaning is that everything is indeed my effect. //39//
Viśvanātha:

That which is the seed, the cause of sprouting—that am I. The reason for this is: whatever might exist without me, whether moving or unmoving, that does not exist at all; the meaning is that it is merely illusory. //39//
Baladeva: And that which is the seed, the cause of germination for all beings, that too am I. The reason for this is: "not without Me.

The meaning is: apart from Me, the Supreme Lord who possesses all potencies, there is no such thing as a being—whether moving or non-moving—that could exist as a reality; it would be merely false. //39//
O scorcher of foes, there is no end to my divine manifestations; this detailed account of my manifestations has been declared by me only in brief. 40.
Śrīdhara: He concludes the meaning of the section with the words "there is no end.
Because His manifestations are infinite, they cannot be described in their entirety;
however, this expansion of manifestations has been declared by way of enumeration and in brief. //40//
Madhusūdana,
concluding the meaning of the section, summarizes his manifestations (vibhūti) with the words "there is no end":
"O scorcher of foes" (parantapa), you who cause distress to others— that is, to enemies such as desire, anger, greed, and the like.
There is no end or limit to my divine manifestations;
therefore, even by the Omniscient One, they cannot be fully known or described, because omniscience has as its object only that which truly exists.
However, this extensive detail of my manifestation has been declared to you by me in brief, as a mere fraction. 40.
Viśvanātha concludes the section: "There is no end"—this extensive detail has been provided merely by way of enumeration, that is, by name alone. //40//
Baladeva: He concludes the section with the words "there is no end.
The detailed exposition (*vistara*) has been proclaimed by way of enumeration (*uddeśataḥ*), that is, by way of a single portion (*ekadeśataḥ*), through a single part (*ekadeśena*). //40//
Whatever being possesses grandeur, beauty, or power, know that to have sprung from but a fragment of my splendor. 10.41
Śrīdhara: Furthermore, he speaks somewhat exhaustively in response to one who is still full of expectation, using the phrase "whatever... whatever.
"Vibhūtimat" means endowed with sovereignty (aiśvarya);
"śrīmat" means endowed with prosperity (sampatti).

Know that whatever being there may be, even if it is preeminent due to some quality such as power or majesty, each and every one of them has arisen from but a fraction of my own splendor and power. //41//
Madhusūdana:
This expression "whatever" (*yad yad*) is stated as an illustration in order to include even those divine manifestations (*vibhūti*) of the Blessed One that have not been explicitly mentioned.
Whatever being (*sattva*) there is—whether a living creature or a manifestation endowed with sovereignty (*aiśvarya*).
Likewise, "śrīmat" means endowed with *śrī*, which is *lakṣmī*, prosperity, splendor, or beauty.
Understand—that is, know—that whatever victory those two possess, which is endowed with an excellence of strength, has arisen from but a fraction of my own splendor and power. //41//
Viśvanātha:
In order to include even those manifestations (*vibhūtayaḥ*) belonging to the three periods of time that have not been explicitly mentioned, he says "whatever...":
"possessing manifestation" (*vibhūtimat*) means endowed with sovereign power (*aiśvarya*).
Śrīmat means endowed with prosperity; ūrjita means superior in strength, power, and so forth; and sattva refers to any substantial entity whatsoever. //41//
Baladeva: To include the manifestations not explicitly mentioned, he says "whatever" (yad yad). "Vibhūtimat" means endowed with sovereignty;
"śrīmat" means endowed with beauty or prosperity; and "ūrjitam" means endowed with strength—whatever being or object exists [is to be understood as such].
"Understand that each and every one of those who have attained perfection has arisen through a portion of my splendor and a fragment of my power; recognize them as such.
Thus, all designations of non-difference are explained by way of being dependent on Him and being pervaded by Him; the designations of Vāmana and others, however, are reconciled accordingly. //41//
Or rather, what is the use of this extensive knowledge to you, O Arjuna?
Pervading this entire universe with but a single fraction of Myself, I stand as the world. 10.42
Śrīdhara: Or rather, what is the use of this display of limited manifestations?
He says "Or rather" (*athavā*) to indicate: "Cast your gaze only upon Me everywhere.
What need have you for the knowledge of many separate things?

Since I alone exist, having supported, held, or pervaded this entire world with but a single part—that is, by a mere portion—there is nothing whatsoever apart from me, according to the Vedic revelation: "All beings are one foot of Him; His three-footed immortal self is in heaven" (Ṛgveda 8.4.17.3). Therefore, the intention is: "What is the use of this limited perception? Rather, maintain the vision of Me everywhere. //42//
Even though the mind runs outward through the doors of the senses,
the Lord taught his sovereign power in the tenth chapter in order to establish the vision of the Master.
Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Yoga of Manifestation," in the *Subodhinī*, a commentary on the *Bhagavad-gītā* composed by the venerable Śrīdhara Svāmī. //10//
Madhusūdana:
Having thus described His manifestation part by part, He speaks of it in its entirety with the words "Or else" (*athavā*).
"Or else" (*athavā*) indicates an alternative view.
What would be gained for you by this extensive knowledge, which remains incomplete?

O Arjuna, it is I alone who stand supporting—upholding or pervading—this entire whole world with but a single portion, a mere fraction; there is nothing whatsoever apart from Me. "A quarter of Him is all this universe... (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.9).
According to the Vedic revelation, "The beings [are] in the three quarters; the immortal is in heaven.
Therefore, the intention is: "What is the use of this limited vision? Rather, everywhere maintain my very own vision. //42//
Some fortunate ones, having fixed their minds upon some part of your infinite form, achieve peace from other afflictions by means of a single drop of nectar trickling from your lotus feet.
Having tasted them repeatedly, my mind becomes intoxicated by the honey.

Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Yoga of Manifestation," according to the distinction of qualified aspirants, in the *Śrīmad-Bhagavad-Gītā-Gūḍhārtha-Dīpikā* (The Lamp Illuminating the Hidden Meaning of the Śrīmad-Bhagavad-Gītā) composed by Śrī Madhusūdana Sarasvatī, disciple of the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya Śrī Viśveśvara Sarasvatī.
Viśvanātha:
What is the use of knowing [these things] individually in great detail? Know them as they are combined; thus he says, "having pervaded" (*viṣṭabhya*).

By a single part—that is, by one part alone, in the form of the Puruṣa who is the inner controller (*antaryāmin*) of *prakṛti*—he has created this world and, because he is its substratum, having pervaded it by means of sustaining and presiding over it, he remains established therein.
As the controller, I am the pervader of that which is controlled; as the cause, I remain after having created that which is pervaded. //42//
Since the entire universe is Śrī Kṛṣṇa alone, one should serve Him with an intellect bestowed by Him; that He alone is the essence of all sweetness—this is declared to be the meaning of the chapter.
Thus, in the *Harṣiṇī* commentary that showers the essence of meaning for those whose hearts are devoted, the tenth chapter has been appropriately concluded for the virtuous. 10.
Baladeva: Having thus described the manifestations (vibhūtis) according to their individual parts, He speaks of them collectively with the words "Or rather" (athavā).
O Arjuna, what purpose is served for you by this extensive knowledge concerning the manifestations, taught separately one by one?

I remain as the creator by virtue of creating, as the sustainer by virtue of supporting, and as the pervader by virtue of pervading—having entered and pervaded the entire world consisting of the conscious and the unconscious, headed by Hara and Viriñci, by means of my single portion called Puruṣa who acts as the inner controller from Prakṛti onwards;

thus, through creation and the other functions, I abide as the creator, the sustainer, and the protector within all things pervaded by me. These acts of creation and so forth are my divine manifestations (vibhūti) within everything that is pervaded by me.
All things, such as sovereignty and the rest, are to be understood as my manifestations (vibhūti). //42//
He from whose mere fragment of power the sun and other luminaries possess such exceedingly fierce brilliance,
and by a portion of whom the entire universe is sustained— that Kṛṣṇa one should worship in the tenth month.
Thus ends the tenth chapter in the commentary on the Śrīmad-Bhagavad-gītā Upaniṣad.
Marīci, Atri, Aṅgiras, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu,
and the highly fortunate Vasiṣṭha were indeed equal to Svayambhū himself.
"There are seven Brahmās"—this is the conclusion established in the Purāṇa.
